utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The cross-examination by Mr. Stamp will now continue. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration you made at the beginning of your evidence to speak the truth continues to apply to that evidence today. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to the TEC, but before I do one question: Minic was the leader of the Working Group that was appointed in June by the party, was he?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. How was the TEC financed, from where did its budget come?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, Mr. Stamp, the Temporary Executive Council was established by Serbia's Assembly, by a decision dated the 28th of December, 1998. It was based on that decision and based on the budget adopted by Serbia's Assembly in relation to the provincial Temporary Executive Council of Vojvodina, the Government of the Republic of Serbia, and the Temporary Executive Council for Kosovo and Metohija. So in answer to your question, it was Serbia's Assembly that adopted the budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did it receive funds, perhaps to augment its budget, did it at all -- receive funds at all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the benefit of the transcript, it says Temporary Executive Council for Vojvodina, Executive Council for Vojvodina. Temporary Executive Council is only in relation to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Executive Council for Kosovo, council and temporary -- which by a decision of Serbia's Assembly is awarded a budget every year. In 1998 the budget was already decided for the work of the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was it partly financed by any companies in Serbia at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I state with full responsibility, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did it receive assistance in any way from companies that were run or managed by members of the party?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless you include the fact that I paid for my own accommodation in the Grand Hotel because I was a company manager at one point in time but not in 1999. I tried to pay for my own accommodation --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- From the budget adopted by the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Please let there be no overlap between counsel and witness, otherwise we can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, just separate lives just the daily allowance. I was receiving my salary as a delegate not even as a minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You had to travel to Kosovo and all over Kosovo many times as a member of the TEC, and you must- I think you will agree with me- have incurred expenses. Who paid those expenses?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a minister in Serbia's government. I had a chauffeur and I had a vehicle placed at my disposal by the Government of Serbia. Me, personally -- are you asking about me?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. And -- but you paid your own hotel accommodation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not personally, as a company manager. Up until October, November, sometime around then. After that, the Executive Council paid for me as well as the other members of the Executive Council who stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You can just answer this question yes or no. Did you indicate to Mr. Curtis when you spoke to him that your expenses on behalf of the TEC or on behalf of your work in the TEC was paid for indirectly by the party by a company associated with the party?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, there are a lot of imprecisions. I saw the note two or three days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time the Working Group of the Executive Council of the Republic of Serbia were there, our expenses were paid by the party company -- well, I'm telling you what I said. I'm just trying to explain, Mr. Stamp, it's not the note, it's what I said. During the time the Working Group of the Socialist Party of Serbia was staying there, the party company, of which I was manager and the Main Board, the founder, paid for all our expenses; that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, I even showed Mr. Curtis the bills.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were sort of joking about how much he was paying and how much I was paying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did you or did the TEC send reports to the president, Mr. Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember. It may have been about education because that's what we often spoke about, Mr. Milutinovic and I, but it's possible we discussed other issues --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- It's just that I can't remember sometimes--

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was asking that P2900 [Realtime transcript read in error "P900"] be brought up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The document you're seeing there, I see that the -- before we get to the document I see that the transcript indicates P900, it's P2900. Could you start by looking at the front page. You might not be familiar with that, Mr. Andjelkovic, but this is a folder cover that we have heard is used by the office of the president of the republic, and it indicates that you sent as president of the TEC this report.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could look --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And it's a report, as you can see, on the engagement of the activities of the TEC from 24th of March to 13 April 1999. This was during the -- this was just at the beginning of the --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So if we look at page 2 on that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We should have P2900 on the screen. I'm looking at the hard copy but what I see on the screen is not what I have for P2900.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you go to page 2 of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just wanted you to have a look at it quickly and tell me if you remember now that you were sending reports to the president?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We sent reports to all sorts of addresses. I do know that I spoke to one of the presidents about humanitarian aid for Albanians in Sajkovac sometime in mid-April. I went to see him for about five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what's the answer to the question? Were you sending reports to the president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were sending information concerning our work to all sorts of addresses. The secretariat was sending out those to the president of the government, the prime minister, the president of the republic, the federal government all sorts of addresses as I say. I'm not saying that we weren't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Andjelkovic, were you sending reports to the president: Yes, no, or don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not on a regular basis, but whenever we felt it was necessary, the secretary, the Executive Council, would send reports to all people in responsible positions in the republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we have a look at page 6 of this document, please, page 6 in the B/C/S and I think it's page 6 as well in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is probably page 7 in the B/C/S copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does no one prepare cross-examination details for you before you come into court and make sure you've got the right references so that we can quickly move through e-court, which is a very difficult thing to do in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The reference is here, apparently there is a mistake. The reference has been prepared as page 6. Apparently there is a mistake, so I'm just trying to find the right one. I'm told it's page 4. Could we move to page 4 on the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just want you to look at it and tell me if you signed and sent off these documents, sent off that cover letter.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't look like my signature, but yes it was sent on the 16th of April, the meeting of the Temporary Executive Council took place, and based on what happened at the meeting the secretariats probably sent this to various addresses including this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, is it your signature or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I see it, it doesn't look like my signature. It was probably signed by the chef de cabinet or someone else. It was certainly sent from the Executive Council to the president of the republic so it doesn't make any difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recognise the stamp on it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what I'm saying. It doesn't make any difference. It was sent from the Executive Council to the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall how frequently you would send reports to the president?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the 16th of April was when the session took place and it was probably right after the session that what was an offer of the Executive Councils was sent by the president of the republic to some other people too [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Whatever it is?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no I wasn't going to. I was just sort of leafing through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. So I take it from what you just said that you don't recall how frequently you sent reports to the president or do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. This is something that was done by the secretariat of the Executive Council. They would draw up collective reports on the work of the Executive Council, and this would then be forwarded to a number of addresses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on to 1D454.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, Mr. Stamp, just a minute, just a minute -- all right. I see it. It's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, could we move on to 1D454.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is not on the list that I sent but I don't see anyone objecting, but it is the Official Gazetted version of P956 which was on the list which I sent. So it's virtually the same document but this is the Official Gazetted version of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a decision on the organisation of the TEC, and I just want to take you quickly to page 2 thereof. You will see -- no, I'm sorry, could we go back to page 1, please. Page 1 of the B/C/S and you will see at the bottom right-hand corner sections 7 and 8 of Article 2, it provides in section 7 that the Executive Council appoints and dismisses senior officers of provincial administrative organs and services. What were the provisional -- provincial administrative organs and services? Did this include the districts in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was a document that was drawn up by the provincial secretariat for regulations in keeping with those drafted by the provincial council of Vojvodina. They believed that some future Executive Council would also have its own administrative bodies. So far they only had secretariats, but those had no jurisdiction over the districts or municipalities or any state institutions in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What you are saying that this was drafted but there were no provincial administrative organs at all that you had any authority over in terms of appointing or dismissing officers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only within the Temporary Executive Council provincial secretariat for regulations and so on and so forth, and the technical services, secretaries, drivers, whatever was there already and whatever had been working for the Executive Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, what were the provincial administrative organs and services in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which temporary organs and services do you mean? You mean the temporary municipal council? What exactly do you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Paragraphs 7 and 8 of section 2 -- Article 2 refers to the provincial administrative organs and services. I'm just asking what were they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no organs and the technical services belonged to the working community and there is a decision adopting just that. This comprised secretaries, drivers, typists. The Executive Council did not have any administrative function; therefore, it did not appoint a single administrative body if that's what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Article 2, paragraphs 7 and 8 are on page 2 of the English, page 1 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So in Article 8 when it says that you are to steer and coordinate the work of these administrative organs and services and monitor their performance, you are speaking about monitoring the performance of your secretaries and drivers, that is what the decision of the -- the gazetted decision was referring to; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that the Assembly gave us no open powers. We put together a decision based on that made by the Executive Council in Vojvodina in the expectation of an agreement, and that powers would be granted that would create the conditions to set up certain bodies, certain administrative bodies, and certain services.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The decision, though, that you're -- we're looking at, it had legal effect; you'll agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense? Yes, if there had been administrative bodies, it would have had, but based on what the Assembly -- what powers the Assembly gave us - and they gave us no powers at all - we could not set up any provincial bodies or administrative bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have nothing further for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Andjelkovic, you were asked yesterday about the handwritten document, which is P1468. Did you have a hard copy of it or were you relying only on what was on the screen?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- I don't know what you mean, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You remember the document you had difficulty reading?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. I wasn't able to read it from that text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you have a hard copy of that document, a paper copy?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have it there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it will be returned to you now, and would you find the page -- it's page 50, I think, in the English in e-court but the number at the end of the references that you were referring to in the B/C/S version was 8450.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance, it's 39 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the trouble with -- it's 39 in e-court, that's fine, but it's not 39 in the hard copy, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have the page, Mr. Andjelkovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's the 12th of August, then, yes, Your Honour, is that what you're referring to, the 12th of August, K022 et cetera. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And does that finish 8450?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And does it include in the lower half the apparent comments of Mr. Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says Mr. Sina -- Sinav. The penultimate S-a-m-a-r -- Samar or Simar or something like that. Maybe somebody can help me out here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You remember yesterday having difficulty reading the second-last line in that section?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you remember that? Now, would you look closely at it again and it will be magnified as far as possible on the screen for you. And tell me whether you see in that line the word "oduzimanje".

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next to whose name, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Andjelkovic, my patience is wearing thin --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the wrong page in B/C/S, it's the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's not page 39? I'd be grateful for accurate information coming to assist us with this exercise. Which page should it be from the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to understand what you want, Your Honour. 8450, the last digits of that page, and now on that page the last line, the penultimate word, what is that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we zoom in on it, please, so that I can see it better? "Nastaviti," continue with -- continue gathering arms, "nastaviti sakupljanje oruzja."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is not the page that I am looking at, but we note what you say about the words that are used in this one. Now, when you say the second-last line, are you referring to what's under the name Minic or are you referring to what's under the name Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the name Minic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the last line there seems to me to read: "Continue with the collection of arms or gathering up of arms."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Right. Now, if we have page 50 of the English on e-court, please, and we pull it up the -- no, we have it now. Thank you. Now, please put on the screen the equivalent B/C/S page, page 40. Now, please magnify the second-last line under the second bottom contributor. Can we magnify it more? Is that it? You can't put the square around the line? You can't draw the dotted line around the line and magnify it? No, no, no, it's the higher part. Now, you've just done it with the wrong part so can you not do it with the right part. No, no, the one above, the section above that, the second-last contributor on the page. No. The one we had great attention paid to yesterday and it's the second-bottom line. That's it. We don't seem to be able to magnify it. Is that the best it can be done? No, that's -- that doesn't matter. It's the B/C/S that matters. Can we fill the screen with the B/C/S and try and magnify that. Thank you. Now, can I ask you the question again. Do you see in the second-last line under Mr. Sainovic's name the word "oduzimanje"?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the penultimate line, through the administrative line, "pojaceti preko administrativne linije," strengthen across the administrative line. Is that it? The second line from the top. Is that what you're referring to, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you see the name Sainovic and you will see that there are one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight lines, so it's the seventh line that I would like you to look at.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven. Project through the administrative line or appear through the administrative line, "pojaviti" or "projektovati."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are you suggesting that that's what the second-last word in that line is?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Pojaviti pojaceti," appear strengthen, "preko" across the administrative line. This last word is probably line, "linija," line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the second-last word is?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Administracija," administration or administrative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You can clear the screen --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first letter is either an O or an A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the second letter?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second letter is either a Q or a D, that's why I thought it was "admi."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's assume the first letter is O and the second letter is D, what would the word be? What's the word?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Oduzimanje."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Taking away, seizing, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or "oduzimanje."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Taking away the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So if that word is "oduzimanje," that means confiscated the line; is that correct? That question's going to sound odd in the translation.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Oduzimanje" is -- means "oduzimanje," taking away, I don't know how to say it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. It was a rather silly question. Right. Now, we can clear that from the screen. You have the hard copy of that document in front of you, P1468, the whole lot?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've seen that on a number -- you've seen it on a number of occasions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, today and today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you saw it four years ago?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I got the impression yesterday you had seen it --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When Mr. Curtis --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I said was very precisely that Mr. Curtis showed it to me like this and I just leafed through it, and I couldn't read it. And I said -- what could I say there and then I answered the questions he asked me, he asked me several questions and that was on the 8th of February and that's what I said yesterday, on the 8th of February, 2003, that is. I didn't have it in my hand so I could study it for an hour or two or three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But in the last couple of days you've been in the position to look at parts of it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, bearing in mind your recollection of the various meetings you went to, whatever the nature of these meetings, does it appear to accurately reflect the names of the people who were meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, only those who spoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was some people from Belgrade who didn't take the floor, so they're not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it accurately reflect the names of the people who spoke? Does it appear to do that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it appear to accurately reflect the subjects that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The subjects were the ones they were, the political situation in the field, on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it, therefore, look like a document prepared by somebody who actually went to these meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly the person went to the meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that -- does it look like a document compiled by somebody who was regularly attending the meetings that you went to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, relatively. It looks sort of regular. They are similar handwritings. There are two handwritings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that. I'm asking you whether the contents of this appear consistent with who went to the meetings, what you discussed so that it appears to have been compiled by somebody -- two people or people who were there.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Bearing in mind what they've noted, have you any idea who the person or persons might have been?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A soldier of some kind. Judging by the handwriting and the qualifications used, this is a military text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Stamp, do you have any questions arising out of any of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Your Honour. Further examination by Mr. Fila:

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Andjelkovic, the Judge asked you what the Prosecutor did not and that is to try to establish the authenticity of the document, to try to do so. Now, when you look at the first page of the document, the first page here, the title page, was that compiled by someone who was at the meeting, printed like that and handwritten down here?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not possible at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did anybody warn you and say that this first page was not authentic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For example, Curtis, the investigator?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Or the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Andjelkovic, you established a moment ago that there were two types of handwriting which means that this was written by two different people?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I see it as I look at the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you look at the topics, the subjects - and this is a question that His Honour asked you just a moment ago - are they all subjects that were all discussed in total or just those of interest to the army?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just the army. There were a lot of humanitarian and social questions that we were interested in, but there's nothing about that here --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Re-examination, but the last question -- the last question was very leading so I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I've got my screen off --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a response to the question put to the witness by the Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. It was a leading question, Mr. Fila. It would be better -- I don't think any harm has been done by that one because the witness has already dealt with it, but please be careful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As far as I can see, the people mentioned here are individuals who were not members of the army. There were much fewer army people?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said yesterday to Their Honours, and that's what I said a moment ago. The people who did not take the floor are not recorded here, but there were civilians and assistant ministers and ministers, and attention is drawn to the civilians, but military terminology is used. The other topics were not discussed, or rather, were not recorded here, whether they were discussed or not I can't say and whether this is an exact report or not, I can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we conclude --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, I want you to be the last to ask, rather than me, any questions of this. But is that not indicative of the fact that the civilians present were involving themselves in military issues, if what you have is civilians recorded as speaking but the issues are military issues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you can see, Your Honour, these were -- some of them were civilian questions and ones I raised at the meeting. Now, what I said -- I spoke at greater length about civilian issues and that's not recorded here and I kept speaking about food supplies, whether a truck could reach a certain village, whether glass could be sent to one village and flour to another village, for example, but this is not recorded here. It doesn't seem to have been of interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I entirely understand that. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At one point Mr. Stamp read out something about 52.000 mattresses or something like that -- rifle --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said yesterday that I asked that these silly things that Rajko was saying because he was always playing up to Slobodan Milosevic, they laughed and said that was not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: From the text you can see that you asked or didn't ask?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't see anything, just a line and then inspection, I spoke about inspection, and said that everything had to be controlled by the state, competent state authorities and inspection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: My last question, and this was something that the Prosecutor asked you: Can this be understood as something which reflects the spirit of the meetings that were held?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, neither by virtue of the comments made by the civilians there or the subjects treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So your answer is no. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That completes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Andjelkovic, that completes your evidence; thank you for coming here to give it. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my last, too, that's the important point. Mr. Milomir Minic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Minic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Fila on behalf of Mr. Sainovic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Minic, I hope you're sitting comfortably.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Give us your name and surname first and which state and party functions you performed in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: My name is Milomir Minic. In 1998 and 1999, I was the deputy of the Socialist Party of Serbia in the Assembly of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and president of a Chamber of Citizens. At the time I was also a member of the Executive Board of the party and member of the Main Board as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what the situation was like in Kosovo and Metohija in the spring and summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: I do know about the situation, it was very difficult, dramatic. We were facing a new situation in Kosovo and Metohija. There was an escalation of terrorism and the so-called KLA held 40 to 50 per cent of the territory. Many communication lines were severed, and in the last three years, even in 1997, 1998, and later on there were a lot of killings, both Serbs and Albanians. The army and police were attacked, and I think that generally speaking the situation could be termed as very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, the situation in Kosovo and Metohija, was it discussed in the party that exerted authority at the level of Serbia and Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Socialist Party of Serbia of the day was the ruling party, although we had a coalition government in the making, and quite certainly the question of Kosovo and Metohija which has its historical dimension is a very complex question. It was a complicated issue, and it was discussed at the Socialist Party of Serbia meetings, assessing the political situation and our initiatives to find a political solution. Through the Government of Serbia we initiated political talks with the Albanian parties in the desire to arrive at a peaceful political solution about a broad-based kind of autonomy, and we undertook many economic measures as well in Kosovo and Metohija. Just to quote a couple of examples the Government of Serbia even by law formed a directorate for the development of the insufficiently developed parts of Serbia and the headquarters of that organisation was in the province, and we were resolute in resolving problems, Albanian children were placing -- facing many problems, and our political stand was that all children regardless of ethnicity had the right to education. An agreement was signed in that respect, I think it might have been mentioned here, between Milosevic and Rugova, and steps were taken to solve these basic problems that the people were facing, along with all the other security problems that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I asked you about the party activities and you're telling me about the state activities, but was a Main Board meeting held?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. There was a meeting of the Main Board held on the 10th of June, 1998. I gave an introductory speech at that session, at that meeting. It had two parts to it. One was the assessment of the political situation, and I gave the features that I will describe to you and then I proposed to the Main Board a political platform about how the Socialist Party of Serbia believed that the difficult problems in Kosovo and Metohija could be resolved through political means.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there a Working Group elected?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: In that same meeting the Main Board of the SPS appointed a three-member Working Group comprising myself, Zoran Andjelkovic, and Dusko Matkovic. I was designated as the leader of that Working Group and my task was to go to Kosovo and Metohija, or rather, our task was to go to Kosovo and Metohija and to try to step-up political activities there working both with Albanians and Serbs because both of those ethnic groups were in a very difficult situation and we did travel there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Since both of us speak the same language, I would kindly ask you to wait between answering my questions to make the job of interpreters easier. Do you know that at the same time the state organs of Yugoslavia and Serbia took measures within their competencies to increase their presence in Kosovo and Metohija and what were their activities?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Well, not only party organs were involved, also the state organs got more active. I know that the Government of Serbia sent to Kosovo a minister for local self rule. His name was Andreja Milosavljevic. I also know that the federal government and federal prime minister Momir Bulatovic sent to Kosovo Nikola Sainovic, vice-president of the federal government. A Ministry of Foreign Affairs also established an office in Kosovo and Metohija and many other assistant ministers travelled to Kosovo and Metohija. So the activity was quite evident and intense.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you explain, or rather, do you know why the federal government sent Nikola Sainovic there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that Nikola Sainovic was federal deputy prime minister in charge of foreign affairs. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had still not used all of its resources, and one of its exclusive powers pertained to foreign affairs. Serbia did not have a minister for foreign affairs. In Kosovo and Metohija, as this Tribunal knows and the entire international community, there was a big question mark. That year, in 1998, a lot of foreign delegations, ambassadors, international dignitaries came to Kosovo and Metohija. They wanted to find out what exactly was happening there, what was the policy of our country, what were the possible solutions; and I think that this decision of the Federal Prime Minister, Momir Bulatovic, was quite a logical one, the one to send Nikola Sainovic down there, so that all of these foreign visitors could have a competent counterpart to discuss these important issues at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. And your Working Group arrived in Kosovo. What did you find there upon your arrival? What was the situation like, I'm referring to your Working Group, Andjelkovic and so on.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Yes. We went for talks in the provincial board or council. As soon as we arrived there, we met a lot of people. We could see that they were afraid, that they couldn't believe what was happening on. It was my impression and the impression of the entire Working Group was that the Serbs were in such a situation that they had to leave Kosovo collectively. About 35 villages in that part of Metohija -- well, the entire territory of 40 per cent but -- is the territory from which Serbs had already left. There was a lot of insecurity, fear, among them. We talked to them, both to Serbs and Albanians. We wanted to encourage the Serbs not to move out, not to resort to self-organisation. We were telling them that it is the state's responsibility to deal with terrorism, that they should be patient, and then we also talked to Albanians, as much as was possible, especially in the portion of the territory where there was no KLA. We wanted to understand the situation as it was, to try to preserve what existed there, to prevent any terrorist activities. That was the essence of our political work. We met with a lot of people and we were facing a very difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You started saying something about the activities of your team, of your Working Group that had been sent by the Main Board of the SPS in the summer of 1998. Can you give us some facts concerning to the three of you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Dusko Matkovic was the director of Sartid and the vice-chairman of the party. He dealt with political issues within the party hypothesis. He had two factories in Kosovo and Metohija one in Vucitrn and one in Gnjilane, and he was the one who tried to assist the most. We came across a lot of people, and it was his task to mostly assist companies because there was a disruption in the production process. People were afraid that the factories would be attacked by terrorists. I remember that we went together to Trepca, Vucitrn, Pec, Gnjilane. Dusko Matkovic was the one who is most involved is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said he had two factories and we are now in capitalist times and we don't want any misinterpretation here.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: No, those two factories were part of the Sartid company, complex, so they belonged to that company. Zoran Andjelkovic was the government minister for youth and he was a people's representative, so to speak. He spent a lot of time out in the field talking to the Albanians. We tried to rebuild mutual trust and to keep the situation under control. As for myself, I mostly met with provincial party leaders, with municipal presidents, and so on, directors of public companies would also come to see me, and this -- these activities develop -- unfolded in a very dramatic situation. Everybody came asking for help. I came -- I worked with AID. We had a very good understanding of the problems in Kosovo and Metohija. Albanian separatists and terrorism exerted enormous pressure on Albanians. A lot of them led normal lives. I remember that about 60 per cent of Albanians went for treatment, received their pensions, and so on, but they obstructed the political life, they refused to join the structures, the official political process; and we wanted to create a Temporary Executive Council and to start reviving political institutions in the province because we saw that as the only possible avenue for re-integrating Albanians into the system, which in turn was supposed to improve the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Minic, was Sartid a state-owned company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. At that time, Your Honour, we already had the Law on Privatisation which had been adopted I think in 1995, or rather, the Law on Companies was adopted in 1995, the Law on Enterprises, pursuant to which all companies were organised as shareholding companies. And I'm not quite certain but I think the state was a shareholder within Sartid, it was a shareholding company and they had investments there. As for the other two factories that I mentioned, they existed within the Sartid concern and they were part of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At the time when you were involved in activities in Kosovo - you being a member of the Working Group - were there meetings held of representatives of various state organs which were working in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I've already told you, as far as we were concerned, we held meetings with the presidents of municipalities, chief, or rather, heads of districts, directors of public companies. So a lot of people who represented the civilian sector, and that was a feature of our political activity because political activity could unfold through meetings and through other means. We also had meetings with the representatives of the army and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you tell us a bit more about that.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: We had a lot of such meetings. When we arrived in Kosovo and Metohija with this approach that I've described to you, there was a huge surprise awaiting us. The KLA had attacked the Belacevac mine. They had ambushed a bus, kidnapped a shift of miners, blocked the mine itself. This mine is located in the outskirts of Pristina. And on the one hand we had a problem with people who had been abducted. I remember this situation well. There was a danger of the entire electrical system of Serbia coming under attack. People called us and we went to police to talk to them, with representatives of the police. We went to see General Lukic and his associates. We also went to see General Pavkovic in his corps to see what could be done. So that was one sort of meetings that we had with them, and there were a number of such meetings held in the similar manner, or rather, maybe -- I can maybe give you two more examples to illustrate this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did these meetings later on grow into regular meetings and where were they held if so?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: The events and activities of the KLA became ever more radical, and there were many things going on, abductions, villages coming under attack, roads being blocked and so on. So there was a need for us to meet more frequently with the representatives of the army and police, to exchange information. I want to be quite sincere and open here and I will say the following: There was so many things going on, and in order to be able to do something efficiently in the political sense, you had to have the right information. Representatives of the army and police had a lot of understanding for this, and we agreed that in the building of the Executive Council we should meet in the evening at around 7.30 to exchange information. That was the building where we mostly worked, where other party people were. There was the news programme at 7.30 in the evening, and we would get a lot of useful information there about what was going on, what was the situation with the roads, and so on. At the time when these frequent meetings started, we had already had some 50 citizens of Serbian ethnicity who had been abducted. We had very unpleasant encounters with their family members, and we were trying to find out from the police and the army whether there was any information about their whereabouts. So we held meetings there, and the nature of these meetings was that they were informational. And I can confirm that they were quite useful for us because we received information there, but these meetings were also useful for the representatives of the army and police because they would learn about how the people felt and this is the information that we provided to them and that was useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were any records kept of the meetings, any minutes? Also, these activities of yourself and the army and police, were they in any way related to the meetings? We are mostly here interested in the nature of these meetings. Were there any formal minutes held? Was there anyone chairing them, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Well, the first meetings were of an informal nature. We were no formal body. I wish to say quite clearly before the Trial Chamber that in these meetings we only exchanged information, no minutes were kept. In these meetings, the participants were different. We from the Working Group, and Nikola Sainovic would attend some meetings and then go back to Belgrade where we had our activities as well. I was busy in the Assembly and some other people would attend the meeting. And then from the police General Lukic would come, General Stevanovic -- General Stevanovic. And then from the state security there were also several people taking turns and coming to the meetings Gajic, Radovic and some others. I think that General Samardzic came once, Jovica Stanisic came twice. So people coming to Kosovo and Metohija would come there as well. To be fully precise, those were the meetings with people discussing the situation in Kosovo and Metohija [as interpreted]. There was no formal procedure. Plans were not reviewed. Decisions were not taken, and the nature of these meetings had no sequences as far as the independent functioning of the army and police was concerned. We held those meetings precisely so that everybody would do their own job and not other people's job, and I think that they were useful. That was the situation in Kosovo and Metohija at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This wasn't precise enough. Were only the initial meetings informal or were all of them informal, we're just clarifying this for the same of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the witness's answer because of the overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For the transcript, Your Honour, I was listening to the B/C/S testimony of the witness and at line 17 of the prior page, that's page 30, I heard him say that they came to discuss the political situation in Kosovo the transcript only says that they came to discuss the situation in Kosovo. I would ask the witness to clarify which it is. It could make a difference, I would imagine, to the analysis of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Minic, what did you say was the nature of the discussions when people like Gajic, Radovic, and Stanisic came and General Samardzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the security organs, people from the state security would give information about the security situation, the activities of the KLA, and so on. The representatives of the army would report on their activities, and then we would give our information. We would tell them what we knew, what we saw as problems, whether there was any specific information. We would exchange comments in those meetings about this very delicate situation. I can tell you that I understood this intervention of the lawyer as wanting me to say that those were meetings where political situations -- situation was discussed. We definitely discussed the security situation there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, the question you posed before that did not get an answer that was heard by the interpreter, that's at line 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Line 20 says only the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the counsel because the witness started overlapping. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're having difficulty because of the failure to observe a pause between question and answer and answer and question, and you need to clarify the position on your previous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you wait until I finish my question otherwise it doesn't get recorded. At one point in time the interpretation was that you said only the first meetings were informal. I'm asking you: Were only the first meetings informal or were all of the meetings informal? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: I said that all of the meetings that we held with the representatives and the police were informal throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us try to clarify that in its entirety. You as a Working Group, all three of you, were you subordinated to anyone in those meetings or was anyone in those meetings subordinated to you, be it politicians, military men, policemen, whoever?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: There was no subordination in relation to anyone. We didn't interfere in other people's work. Our political activity implied that we were in a position to talk to people, to present our views, to exchange information that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You told us about what work you did in that period. You were the president of one of the two councils of the Federal Assembly, that was one of your roles. I think you are informed enough to answer this question. Was there a constitutional and legal basis to use the VJ and the MUP in the anti-terrorist operation that occurred in the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You described the meetings that you attended --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's very difficult to object because of translations, object before the question goes in and the answer goes in, but I'm not sure that this was notified that he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wouldn't worry about it because it's valueless evidence the way it's been given. His answer "yes" is of no value on the question which Mr. Fila posed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you explain what exactly you base your answer on, the previous answer, when you said yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on now. The objection is that you did not notify the Prosecution that this would be a subject that you would be raising with this witness. What's your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, generally speaking, I said I would be asking questions about his functions and what he knew about that, because that was within his job description. He was the president of one of the two Executive Councils. He had the highest-ranking role in the Federal Assembly of Yugoslavia. I said he'd be speaking about the situation in Kosovo in 1998. The VJ and the MUP were used in 1998; therefore, given his position, he should know. There's no need for me to emphasise the fact that the president of the Executive Council would be in a position to know. I don't think I'm outside of the framework envisaged by 65 ter in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We note that the objection is taken on the basis that this was not notified, and nothing that Mr. Fila has said gives any indication that it was notified as a subject; but in any event, there is a more fundamental reason why this evidence is inadmissible. There is no established qualification on the part of this witness to answer the question put. We do not agree that the grounds advanced by Mr. Fila for saying that he could express an opinion on this matter, on which we could rely have any foundation. So please proceed to something else, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's just for the transcript, line 23, 22, page 33, it reads that he was the president of one of the two Executive Councils and he was the president of two councils of the Federal Assembly of Yugoslavia, which is the supreme legislative body of this particular country. So I think that qualifies him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A chamber, it's not exactly a council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We understand that he's the president of the Chamber of Citizens; that was the evidence which he gave. But we're aware of that in making the decision that we've made.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not objecting about you, Your Honour, it's about the transcript because instead of "chamber" it said something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You described the meetings that you attended back in 1998. Did you hear of anyone calling the meetings you described earlier the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Maybe back in September there were people who referred to those meetings as meetings of the Joint Command; however, those of us who were involved in those meetings - and I mean our Working Group - never referred to those meetings in that way and there was no way we ever could, simply because the meetings were of a nature that I already described.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How long did these meetings continue to be held?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: These meetings were taking place intensively in the second half of July, in August, and in September. They became rarer in October, considerably rarer. I think it was in late October that they stopped taking place altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said you weren't there all the time. You were absent a number of times, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: In September for about 15 days, in October for about 15 days. Yes, I was away because work over at the Federal Assembly was quite intense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Minic, please try to help me a little more. You were asked if you heard of anyone calling the meetings the Joint Command, and your answer is: "Maybe back in September there were people who referred to those meetings as meetings of the Joint Command." Now, what do you mean "maybe" and who were the people that maybe referred to these meetings as meetings of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't remember the specific people - I think they were from the army - however, when I arrived in The Hague I received documents from the Defence team. I tried to analyse a particular document and a particular record. I realised there was a reference there to the last meeting with President Milosevic, where a report was submitted on the implementation of the plan for anti-terrorist struggle. I studied the record closely and I tried to think back as hard as I could to remember what exactly went on at the meeting. I think General Pavkovic mentioned that, General Lukic as well, in their contributions, General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you are saying that at a meeting that Mr. Milosevic presided over, both General Pavkovic and General Lukic mentioned the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so, but I didn't exactly gather, based on that particular record, what this was a reference to, the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I asked you about during those meetings that you had in Kosovo. Was the term mentioned then, during those meetings, because I think that's what the Presiding Judge is asking?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: During the meetings themselves -- I don't know that anyone mentioned the term during the meetings, the meetings that we held. For us, this -- these were meetings with the army and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was Sainovic's role in Kosovo in the summer of 1998 prior to the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Nikola Sainovic, as I've already pointed out, there were many people in Kosovo at the time, foreign delegations, ambassadors, and the federal government dispatched him to Kosovo to talk to those delegations. He was in charge of the talks for the most part. I remember that he had a considerable number of meetings with Ambassador Hill, who was the US Ambassador to Macedonia. He often travelled to Kosovo, and I think that was Sainovic's responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Sainovic's job in relation to the arrival of the OSCE people or the representatives of the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Nikola Sainovic was appointed by the federal government president of the Commission For Cooperation with the OSCE. This was a commission set up by the federal government and it comprised mostly ministers from the federal and republic government. Our country signed an agreement with the OSCE, and Nikola Sainovic was in charge of coordinating all activities in terms of seeing the agreement through, seeing it implemented in its entirety. We had a positive outlook on that mission because the role of the mission was to verify the situation that prevailed, to create conditions for a political process to get underway.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Nikola Sainovic's activity after the beginning of the war about Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: When the war broke out, everything had to be organised in a different way. Everyone had a lot of different responsibilities. As for Nikola Sainovic, I think his involvement in Kosovo was about a very important meeting or talks, if you like, with Mr. Ibrahim Rugova. The situation was very difficult and we assessed that this was of the utmost importance for our country. We use to see Nikola in the party during the war and he told us about his intense activity about organising these meetings and for those meetings to eventually take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As usual, I've only used up 45 minutes for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Stamp -- sorry, sorry, I didn't pay attention to possible cross-examination by Defence. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Minic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Minic, throughout the NATO intervention between the 23rd of March and sometime around mid-May, you took part in so-called meetings of the country's leadership, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Minic, what was the basic reason for these meetings, if you can tell us, please? Just make a pause before you start your answer.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: I remember the meetings. There was a war on, and this was the principal reason for the meetings. As far as I can remember, there were a number of those meetings in March, I think as many as three in March, four in April, two in May, but the state of war that had been declared was the principal reason for those meetings to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Those meetings were recorded by the television, weren't they? What was the reason for you holding those meetings, the TV people, the TV crew recording those meetings, and then the meetings being shown on the evening news by TV Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: In my understanding, there were two different purposes for these meetings, the first being to briefly inform everyone that the situation in the country, about how our forces were holding up, about problems with supplies. There were huge problems with electricity, for example. There were brief comments offered because the way our work was organised implied that everyone should do their own job. You asked me this question about the meetings being recorded. That's true. My personal opinion is - although nobody actually said that at any of the meetings - was that the meetings were recorded and shown on TV. There was a brief summary of these meetings, and this was supposed to send a message through to the people of Serbia to the effect that the country's leaders were hard at work and that they -- they were at work defending their country. We had bitter historical experience back from 1941; on the 6th of April our country was attacked and the government on that same day simply fled the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Minic, how long were these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: They were brief, up to half an hour perhaps. I remember that meetings were held at Beli Dvor during air-strikes. I remember that security people sometimes walked in on our meetings warning us that it would be wise idea to end our meeting because outside the bombs were falling.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In answer to my previous question what you said was in reference to the fact that when hostilities broke out on the 6th of April, 1941, when the Second World War began, the entire government led by the king himself left Serbia and left Serbia's people at the mercy of the German occupier. Is that what you had in mind when you said that you wanted to show the people that the country's leaders at those difficult moments were still in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: I think I've answered that one already. It was a bitter experience from the 6th of April that taught us this. The entire government and the king himself fled to Cairo, Egypt.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Minic, who called these meetings, these leadership meetings [indiscernible] sessions?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: The meetings were called by President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: They were all held at Beli Dvor, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm following on the screen. Yes, they were all held at Beli Dvor, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Minic, for the most part the people being called to those meetings were from the federal bodies and from the republic bodies, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to President Milosevic, other representatives of the federal bodies at these meetings were the Federal Prime Minister, Momir Bulatovic; Defence Minister Pavle Bulatovic; foreign minister Zivadin Jovanovic. As for the Assembly, both presidents of the Assembly were at the meeting, myself and Bozovic on behalf of Serbia. There was the president of the republic, Milan Milutinovic, and the president of the Assembly Dragan Tomic as well as Marjanovic. I'm thinking about that first meeting and who -- General Ojdanic may have been at the first meeting, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Dragan Tomic was president of which Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Assembly of the Republic of Serbia, the national or People's Assembly of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And Bozovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Srdjan Bozovic was the president of the Chamber of the -- the republics of the Federal Assembly, it's the upper Chamber. The Assembly has two Chambers: The Citizens' Chamber and the Chamber of the republics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So I follow Bozovic okay. Tomic remind me or explain more fully what Tomic was president of.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dragan Tomic was the president of the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean he was the president of both houses together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Assembly of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia has two Chambers, and Serbia's Assembly only has one Chamber. There are 250 deputies and representatives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So your position as president of the Chamber of Citizens was a federal position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's probably my mistake but I had not appreciated that. Thank you. Is this a suitable --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Minic, you said that General Ojdanic was probably present at the first meeting. What about the other meetings? Was there ever anyone from the army or the police attending these meetings, the so-called leadership meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What about this body, did it ever have anything to do with defence-related matters in terms of command? Were there any discussions about that or did it deal in a very general way with the situation in the country which arose as a result of the NATO air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: These meetings had nothing to do with defence-related matters in the sense of command, but, as I've already pointed out, those were brief working meetings. In addition to President Milosevic, the one who spoke the most was Mirko Marjanovic. We were facing huge problems with electricity supplies, because NATO's bombs were targeting our energy supplies. Certain types of bombs were dropped and there was the problem of supplies. It was one of the chief issues. Momir Bulatovic sometimes spoke, Zika Jovanovic spoke but these meetings did not review issues related to the country's defence in terms of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At those meetings towards the very end in May, you discussed the country's reconstruction after the air-strikes with Mr. Mrkonjic and Dejan Kovacevic who was a construction minister, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Yes, sometime in the second half of May we were working on a plan for the country's reconstruction. When NATO's aggression came to hold a programme got on the ground immediately. About 80 bridges had been destroyed in Serbia. The construction minister Dejan Kovacevic and Milutin Mrkonjic came to one of these meetings and they were in charge of the country's reconstruction especially as far as destroyed buildings were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Minic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions from me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Minic, we have to break at this stage for a half-hour. The -- if you leave the courtroom with the usher, he will show you where to wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume at 20 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Minic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Lukic -- by Mr. Ivetic on behalf of Mr. Lukic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I should be fairly brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Minic, I just want to ask you about the item that you testified about at page 36 of today's transcript, this document of a meeting with President Milosevic, wherein there were references to a Joint Command. And first of all, am I correct that apart from seeing the references to the Joint Command in the document itself, you did not have an independent recollection of General's Perisic, Pavkovic, or Lukic actually using that term. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: I saw the records and I said that I tried to reconstruct the meeting, and I think that when at the meeting they spoke to the struggle against terrorism, General Lukic and General Pavkovic had in mind their own commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, allow me to ask for Exhibit P2166 to be called up, and, Mr. Minic, when this document comes on the screen I'd like to ask you to take a look at it and advise me whether in fact this is the document that you are referring to that you had reviewed and about which you are talking about now.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: It's in English here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Sir.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, with respect to this meeting, you are listed as one of the persons being present. The question I want to ask you is: Do you recall if you were ever asked to review the minutes of the meeting for their accuracy and to adopt the same, following the meeting having taken place?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: No. I saw these minutes in The Hague for the first time. I've never seen them before. I understood it that we were at a meeting with President Slobodan Milosevic, whereas when I received these minutes and looked at them for the first time I gathered that I had taken part in the meeting of the operative staff for the suppression of terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija. So not then and not now do I know what the operative inter-resources staff was and who its members were and what its role was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, do you recall who took the minutes of this meeting from your review of the document? And perhaps -- well -- actually, I'll withdraw the question. Let's make this -- let's short-circuit this. If you can look to the last page of the exhibit, both in B/C/S and in the English. Sir, I'll just ask you to look at this last page and indeed it lists the minutes being compiled by a Lieutenant-General Slavoljub Susic. Do you recall whether General Susic was a general in the MUP or in the army?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: General Susic was a general in the army and chef de cabinet of the president of the republic, both I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, at line 17 of page 45 it says chef de cabinet of the president, in B/C/S it was "sef vojnog kabineta," chief of the military president which can be in fact verified from the first page of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Minic, could you repeat your description of the position held by General Susic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that he was the chef -- chief of the military cabinet of the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can look at the middle of page 7 of this document, both in the B/C/S and the English, I'd like to focus on the half page or so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you move on, the answer you gave was chief of the military cabinet of the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I think it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that would suggest of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
