utterances.text: Now, as I said, I'd like to move to the middle of page 7 of the document, both in the B/C/S and the English to the small section that relates to Mr. Lukic's discussions at this meeting. And, sir, if I could direct your attention to the -- the only reference to Joint Command is there in the preamble where it says - and I now quote the English whereby hopefully it's the same as the Serbian, I haven't had an opportunity to double-check everything to detail about it. But it says in English: "Major-General Sreten Lukic submitted a report on the work of the Joint Command for KiM, or KiM." The question I have for you, sir: Do you recall that Sreten Lukic actually stood up and said these exact words verbatim: "I, Sreten Lukic, will present a report on the work of the Joint Command for KiM"?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I think that at the meeting itself - and I said here in court that in looking at these minutes I tried to reconstruct the meeting - I think and I'm almost sure that General Sreten Lukic was not supposed to submit a report on the Joint Command I think. I don't think that was scheduled, although it was a long time ago. And I think he spoke about the implementation of the joint plan of the struggle against terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir, for clearing that up for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour, and I thank the Court for its indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Minic, you will now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Since we are on 2166, if we go to page 9 in the English, which is page 10 in the B/C/S -- now I think we are looking at the bottom of page 10 in the English -- sorry, at the bottom of page 9 in the English. And it records here the conclusion of your presentation, and you having studied the document recently, you'll remember that your presentation occupies two pages in these minutes. And it says here: "In conclusion Milomir Minic proposed the following: The operation staff should provide an assessment of how successfully the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija had fulfilled the authorisations conferred upon it." And then it goes on to number 2. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: I did make a similar proposal because I took the floor at the meeting, at President Milosevic's office, and I've already told the Court that I didn't know that an operative staff existed. Now, after the -- speaking about the political situation in Kosovo and Metohija and after the plan's realisation, I did make a proposal, but the proposal that I made is not what it says in this text. I didn't utter two words that are here. I didn't give the term "operative staff" because I really didn't know that that staff existed as such and that I was taking part in a meeting, as I see it written down up here in The Hague when I received this material. And secondly, I never said Joint Command for KiM. I remember very well -- I remember that very well, and that's what I'd like to state here before the Court. That within the frameworks of this text I presented two things. One was my opinion and one was a proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: And my opinion --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just wanted to know if you said anything about the Joint Command, and I take it your answer is --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: What I wanted to say here, if I might be allowed to respond, I'd like to say what I actually said, to tell you what I actually said, if that's of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I made an observation and it was the following. I said: I consider that both the command of the Army of Yugoslavia and the command of the Ministry of the Interior, in the struggle against terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija worked in the best possible way under the given circumstances in the province, the prevailing circumstances in the province. And they showed a high degree of responsibility and selflessness. And I proposed that their work be assessed and evaluated as such at this meeting. And I'm speaking under oath now. What I've just said is under the solemn declaration. I think it is my debt to truth. Now, how it came to be recorded in the minutes in this way, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, it's also recorded in the minutes at page 12 of the English and page 13 in the B/C/S version and I'll just read it to you that President Milutinovic supported the proposal for conservation of the continued status of the Joint Command. Milutinovic believes that the Joint Command should continue functioning for a while. And it also says at page 13 in the English and page 13 to 14 in the B/C/S that Deputy Prime Minister Sainovic agreed with the opinion that the viability of the continued activity of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija in its present composition should be re-evaluated. Did you hear either of them using the term the "Joint Command" in these minutes which were presented by the chef de cabinet of the president?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: I said that I analysed this meeting and I would like to be able to give a precise answer, but the truth of the matter is that I just don't remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: -- So believe me when I say that I just don't remember that they uttered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In this -- in these minutes at page 8 to 9 in the English and also page 8, 9, and 10 in the B/C/S, which you reviewed recently, you spoke for a long time about the conditions on the ground in Kosovo in respect to what the army and the police had achieved. It's -- your presentation is prefaced with these words, that Milomir Minic provide a comprehensive review of the implementation of the plan for suppressing terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija. Well, having reviewed the document and seeing the contents of your review, can I ask you: Where did you get this information from?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Well, I said at the beginning of my testimony, Mr. Prosecutor, that we held meetings with the representatives of the Army of Yugoslavia and representatives of the Ministry of the Interior, and we, within the space of those three months, were all over Kosovo. We talked to the Albanians, to the Serbs, to the people who had been abducted. We went to villages where our army had de-blocked the villages. So this political assessment, this political appraisal of the situation, which was a long one and I think I spoke even longer, and General Pavkovic summarized the results and activities of the army. General Lukic did this too. And I tried to give an overall assessment of those three months there which would be realistic, and that was at a time when the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement was signed and when we expected that we would certainly move towards a normalisation of the situation and unleashing of the political process. And I tried in a synthetic way in a summary form and precis -- may I just be allowed to finish. It was very obvious. Let me give you some examples --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I merely asked where the information came from and I think you've answered that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Minic, have you seen a signed copy of the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I haven't seen the signed agreement. It appeared as a document, an 11-point document of the Government of the Republic of Serbia, so that's the document I saw in that form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where did you see that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was published, it was considered by the government. It was reviewed at our meeting of the SPS, Executive Board, and so on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement by the Serbian government set out in 11 points on the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what you're referring to is a policy statement by the government. You're not referring to the actual agreement itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, that's how the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement was presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it was just your reference to it being signed struck me as possibly important since we've been very anxious to see a signed copy of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see the agreement, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who invited you to this meeting that you are speaking about?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: I was invited to the meeting by the secretary of the president of the republic, her name was Mira, and she told me that the president had scheduled a meeting about Kosovo and Metohija two or three days before the meeting was actually held, and that I should inform Zoran Andjelkovic and Dusko Matkovic to attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in the invitation were you told that you would have to give a presentation?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Well, at meetings of that kind, nothing special was stated in that way. I spoke about the political situation. There were two or three meetings like that. And Milosevic remembers that, or rather, I remember Milosevic as having said in his introduction that Pavkovic would be taking the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I was coming to that. In his introduction - and this is at page 1 of the English - it is recorded that Mr. Milosevic informed the members about the agenda and the order in which the participants would speak: Generals Pavkovic and Lukic, followed by yourself. So were you aware of this agenda that you were slated to speak, and you can tell us if you were, yes; if you were not, no.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Well, I had expected to speak because I led the Working Group of the political -- of the SPS party of Serbia with respect to Kosovo and Metohija and the very difficult situation that the province was facing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said -- I think it was in answer to the -- a question by the Presiding Judge earlier that you think perhaps General Pavkovic and General Lukic mentioned the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: I said that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Go on --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: May I continue? I said that in reading the minutes, in reading the minutes, I felt -- well, I remember the minutes. And I think that it said in the minutes that in the name of the Joint Command General Pavkovic submitted a report or spoke and the Joint Command of MUP - and I've already answered this question put to me by one of the Defence counsel - it was strange to me -- well, I understood it that General Pavkovic was talking about the activities and effects of, or rather, operations of the Army of Yugoslavia in Kosovo and Metohija and that General Lukic tabled a report on the activities of the police --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, very well, thank you --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: That's what I think. Perhaps if you just bear with me for a moment longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I want just to move away from that document. I understand you are saying that you cannot recall anyone mentioning the Joint Command. In respect of those meetings that you were attending regularly from, say, July going on to about October in Kosovo, did you hear anybody refer to those meetings as the Joint Command, as meetings of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: As to those meetings -- well, I think I've already answered that question but I can repeat my answer if you like. At the meetings that we held, about those meetings, nobody said that they were meetings of the Joint Command. It was only later on in the process with Slobodan -- in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic here in The Hague I saw that there were some speeches being made or statements where the Joint Command was mentioned, but it wasn't the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. But -- okay. While you were down in Kosovo working in 1999, did you hear the expression "Joint Command" being used in respect to any organisation -- sorry, not 1999. In 1998.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: In 1998 I was in Kosovo. I was not in Kosovo in 1999. Perhaps a few words, if I might be allowed to say them. In Kosovo and Metohija in 1998, what existed was the Pristina Corps command and the forward command post of the 3rd Army from Nis, led by General Samardzic. That's what existed, and there was a forward command post I think it was probably in Djakovica, too. I think that the police had some sort of organisation which was referred to as the staff so that -- well, we didn't deal with this. We respected them highly. I'm speaking in my own personal name. We met these people in Kosovo as commanders and soldiers. Now, how they commanded, what the organisation was like, we as the political activists did not enter into matters of that kind. They helped us a great deal by providing us with information and by the very fact that we could talk to them to see where everything was going, where the security situation was going for us to be able to take an action on a political level.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In 1998, in the course of your work in Kosovo, did you hear the expression "Joint Command" being used in reference to any of the organs that were involved in the work that you were doing down there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Me hearing this -- no, I'm trying to remember now. I didn't hear it. Perhaps I saw it on some paper concerning to -- concerning the security situation. Maybe I saw this written, this Joint Command, but I never heard it, no, because we, Mr. Prosecutor, did not deal with the command issues. This was such a difficult situation that we simply did not get involved in this. We went to assist the people to return Albanians to the villages, and yes we held meetings with the representatives of the army and police, as I have explained to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Earlier today, Mr. Minic, you were asked about this document and you said that once you saw it: "I studied the record closely and I tried to think back as hard as I could to remember what exactly went on at that meeting. I think General Pavkovic mentioned that," that's Joint Command, "General Lukic in their contributions, General Perisic." That's what you told us earlier today. That's not what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- You're telling us now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as I have stated here before you, I have attempted to remember. This was indeed long time ago. There are two matters here in the minutes, how General Pavkovic was announced and what he actually said as well as how General Lukic was announced and what he subsequently said. When General Pavkovic spoke, we spoke of these commands as we perceived them, and I took it to mean -- and believe me, I never took it to mean that they had some Joint Command. If you permit me. In various contributions of General Pavkovic, it says in one of the pages- and I know this for a fact- in the realisation of the plan a good cooperation was established --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's your recollection that we were asking you about at that point and it's your recollection you were giving us. Now, you do not appear to be saying the same thing now; that's all I'm asking you. You seem to have had a recollection of General Pavkovic and General Lukic mentioning the words "Joint Command."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is truly my wish to describe how I perceived it. It is one thing how they were announced in the minutes and then what they subsequently said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it's what they said that you were being asked about. Just concentrate on the particular point. Why did you earlier tell us that you thought Pavkovic and Lukic and Perisic mentioned the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have said that I received these minutes here, and that document has three dimensions: How they were announced, what they said, and that they spoke about cooperation. General Pavkovic and General Lukic in this note - and I listened to them in that meeting as well but it was a long time ago - both of them, both generals, said that a cooperation had been established at a professional level between the units of the Army of Yugoslavia and the Ministry of the Interior in the implementation of the plan on anti-terrorism activities. Perhaps I wasn't fully precise in phrasing this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I want to give you every opportunity to be clear about this. You see, the reference they made to their respective performances against terrorism you have a clear recollection of. But your answer earlier this morning was: "I think General Pavkovic mentioned that and General Lukic and General Perisic." Now, why did you say that to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in the sense that in the minutes they were presented in this way. I truly wish you -- want you to believe that I did my best to remember this, but it was my understanding that General Pavkovic spoke about this. He had a corps, he had the 3rd Army, he had a General Staff, and he spoke of his activities, and that General Lukic spoke about the MUP activities and that they cooperated between themselves. And that the minutes depicted them -- and I tried to remember this. When President Milosevic introduced speakers- and I remember this well, I know how he chaired meetings- he would normally say: General Pavkovic has the floor now. He wouldn't say: A member of the Joint Command. And then he would say: General Lukic has the floor. And then when he would give the floor to me he would say: It is now the president of the Chamber of Citizens who has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see after you gave that answer I asked you: "So you're saying at a meeting that Mr. Milosevic presided over both General Pavkovic and General Lukic mentioned the Joint Command." And you started your answer by saying: "I think so ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember. Perhaps I wasn't fully specific about them being presented in the minutes as speaking on behalf of some kind of a Joint Command. And, Mr. Presiding Judge, in response to a question from the Prosecutor I also said that I wasn't sure about ever hearing about the Joint Command, and this is what I found strange in the minutes because I had been present in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. But -- and that is why I reminded you earlier that in answer to the question from the Judge you said that you thought Generals Lukic and General Pavkovic had spoken about the Joint Command. Anyway, withdrawn. Let's move on. You said you might have -- you didn't hear about the Joint Command in regard to anybody that was involved in Kosovo in 1998 but you might have seen it on some document. Perhaps -- you said perhaps you might have seen it on some document or anything like that -- or something like that. Would you -- if you saw this expression "Joint Command" on some document, wouldn't you have inquired what it was about and did you inquire what it was about if you saw it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to be as specific as possible, and I apologise to Their Honours and the Presiding Judge. No, we did not inquire about the Joint Command. We did not deal with the command at all. We did not inquire. We knew that the army had its own command, and I told you that we had heard about how many locations there were where there was a command, but we did not make any inquiries because that wasn't up to us, that wasn't our task. We dealt with some other very complex issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was merely asking about your response to me when you said that perhaps you might have seen the expression "Joint Command" on some documents. If you saw the expression "Joint Command" on documents in 1998, wouldn't you as leader of the Working Group have made efforts to discover what this Joint Command was?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Well, I thought that that was some kind of an army command. I did not understand it in any other way. We didn't look into it to tell you the truth. We didn't deal with it. This wasn't our topic, this wasn't our issue. I would have said so had it been otherwise here before the Trial Chamber. I had gone there to help; that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let me just understand you now. You are saying that you heard or saw the expression "Joint Command" in 1998 while you were working in Kosovo? You knew that there was an organ that was called the Joint Command in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: I didn't, no. I didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You recall that there was a meeting held by President Milosevic in July 1999 [as interpreted] where the leaders of the police and the army attended and where Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Milutinovic also attended in which General Pavkovic presented a plan for resolving the security situation in Kosovo. You remember that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: I remember that meeting; I took part in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to clarify, Mr. Staff, are you asking about July of 1999, as the transcript reflects, because I don't think that's the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, in July of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Prosecutor asked you about attending a meeting in July of 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think the witness has clarified that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to the implementation of this plan, Sreten Lukic - that's General Lukic - was questioned about it when he spoke to representatives of the ICTY. And he said that as far as he remembered it was Mr. Minic, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Matkovic, Mr. Andjelkovic, who composed the Joint Command. And he also said, also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the reference? Could we see it on the screen? Could the witness read this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is P948 --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now would you please show all of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a matter for Mr. Stamp to decide how he presents his questions. You decide that, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, it's P948 and I'm referring to page 70 and 71. There's no need to show it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, he said that those four persons composed the Joint Command and it also included himself, that's General Lukic, and General Pavkovic as regular members in charge of carrying out the tasks related to the anti-terrorist actions. Now, do you know of any reason that General Lukic would have to believe that you were a member of a body called the Joint Command in which both himself and General Pavkovic were also members?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any reason. I don't know about this statement. All I can say here is that Zoran Andjelkovic, Dusko Matkovic, and myself were never members of any command or Joint Command in Kosovo and Metohija in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How about Mr. Sainovic, do you know of any reason, anything that Mr. Sainovic did why General Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Neither Mr. Sainovic. Neither Mr. Sainovic, as I have said already. Mr. Sainovic had been sent by the federal government as the government representative for foreign affairs, and, Mr. Prosecutor, I have stated here loud and clear that we, members of the Working Group, held meetings with the representatives of the army and police in July, August, and September.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: At that time it was an informal body where we exchanged political information.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to object. I apologise, but Mr. Stamp is reading incorrectly the words of Lukic. Please look at page 70 of the document to verify whether that's exactly what it says, because had he not referred to the document he would have been in position to say anything he wanted, but if he did then he has to abide by what is stated in the document. The pages are 20 to 23 -- I apologise, page 70, 20 to 23. If he is referring to the words of Lukic, he has to do so accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's page 70, 20 to 25, and page 71, page 1 to page 6 -- sorry, lines 1 to line 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry, you have answered the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Can we see these pages, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both of my texts are in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's because --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I have another objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's because we are looking at it. Just give us a moment to do that. You can take it off the screen now. Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the extent that I understood your ruling, the statement of one accused cannot be used against another accused. And what Mr. Stamp is doing is precisely that in relation to Mr. Sainovic, whom I defend here. This is how I see it. And if I'm wrong, I apologise, both to you and to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All that Mr. Stamp is doing is using this to refresh the witness's memory with a view to getting evidence from the witness, not to directly use the statement at this stage. So there's no problem with that, nothing inappropriate about following that course. And for what it's worth, my own view is that the statement does say what Mr. Stamp claimed. There may be other arguments in the way in which question and answer came, but that is undoubtedly one view of what could be formed in what was in that section of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You just said that you don't I think -- words to the effect that you don't know what -- on what basis it could be said that Mr. Sainovic was a member of the Joint Command. Can I ask you this: Were you in Kosovo in 1999 during the -- during March to June 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So if I represented to you that Mr. Sainovic attended meetings of the senior members of the MUP in Kosovo in that period in 1999, would you know about those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: I have stated here that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'll therefore refrain from asking about events in Kosovo in 1999. You recall, however, that you met from time to time with President Milutinovic in respect to events in Kosovo during 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: I met with President Milutinovic not only by myself but also with others attending concerning the implementation of the education agreement in Kosovo and Metohija in the final stages. It was our firm intention, both of President Milutinovic and Serbia, to have this signed agreement implemented and to have all children in Kosovo and Metohija have access to proper education --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: -- And the implementation of that agreement --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Did you have meetings with himself or others or attend meetings with himself and others in Kosovo in respect to the security situation in Kosovo, and that's in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: In 1998, perhaps I went once with President Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I see if I could refresh your memory. I would like to bring up P2805. These are minutes of a meeting of the MUP staff --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: It's in English -- I see the first page. It's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. They are minutes of the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija. And if we move to page 2 of the English and e-court page 3 of the B/C/S we could see who attended this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: If I may be given a moment to look at it, please. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The president, the minister of interior, the leadership of the police, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Andjelkovic, Mr. Matkovic, the assistant chiefs of the SUP. You recall that meeting? It's the 11th -- sorry, it's the 5th of November, 1998, in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: If you can scroll down a bit, please. I think it was the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But you recall the meeting? That's what I'm asking?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You also remember that General Pavkovic was there. So you have not only the leadership of the police but also the army. General Pavkovic and 13 representatives of the Pristina Corps were present. Now, if we could look at page 3 in the English, page 4 in the B/C/S. If we could expand the second paragraph in the B/C/S version. I'd like you to just read that section.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: From which point?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we pan out on the page. I'm told that in Cyrillic it's at the top of the page. I'll just read it to you because -- I'm speaking from line four in Cyrillic. Can you read it aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: From which point --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: From the --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: It says: "The Army of Yugoslavia ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, start from the sentence before that.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: "This political process ..." That's what I have on my screen as the first full sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Go on, please do that.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: "This political process shall last for a long time and a difficult one. The Siptars and the Americans will insist on a different political solution for the status of Kosovo but we will oppose that. As for the Army of Yugoslavia and police, everything remains the same. Joint Command, VJ units are not withdrawing and police forces have been reduced only by the members who have had already withdrawn. Police and the army continue to have the right to intervene if they are attacked."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry. The president of the republic referred to Joint Command according to the minutes of this meeting. Did you hear him say that at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you hear him describing the position that he expected the Kosovar Albanians and the Americans, regardless of what he decided to term the Kosovar Albanians as, but did you hear him describing the position that he thought the Kosovar Albanians and the Americans would take at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: I was at the meeting, as you can see from the minutes, but I don't remember what he said, truly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Can we look at 11 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As I see that Mr. Stamp is moving from this document now, there is just one thing, in line -- 64, 17, the witness has said this meeting was in relation to Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement, and I believe the transcript says it was -- I lost it: "I think it was Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the sense is the same. Your point is noted. Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we move on to P1198, P1198. We could move straight to page 2 -- well, let's look at it first.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's a document -- and I'll just wait until it gets on to the screen. This is a document which I represent to you was taken from the Executive Council building in Pristina by investigators on the 1st of August, 1999. It purports to be a report of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, strictly confidential, dated the 23rd of November, 1998. And without going into all of the report, I represent that it includes a description of the security situation in the region and the activities of the KLA or what is described as the terrorists against the VJ and the MUP and the population and the engagement of VJ and MUP units. Do you recall ever receiving a document like this -- or this document while you were in Kosovo in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Can we please go through the whole document? All I can see here is half a page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How many pages are there, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I could please see the end of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we go to the last page, to the last page of the document. That's it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not the end, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you scroll up slightly you'll see that it looks like the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Could we just go back to the first page of the document then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the question you were asked was: Do you recollect ever seeing a document like that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's go to the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I could have it in Serbian, please. The Serbian is gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It should be back now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, the previous page, page 1 in e-court on the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You'll see there is handwriting there on the cover page of the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you read it, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: "To Mr. Milomir Minic, personally."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So if we now look at page 3 of that document in -- on the English version and also on the e-court version, in section 2 where it discusses or where it's headed "terrorist action," you see that it sets out a variety -- well, three or four events that occurred within the previous 24 hours. You see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you receive reports of this nature on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I wasn't in Kosovo and Metohija in November. I think the activity ended on the 28th of October. However, members of the Working Group occasionally received documents like these. That is why I said I had the impression that I saw the expression for the first time being used somewhere, not actually heard it used. This was the sort of document that we occasionally received from the VJ. As far as I remember, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Minic, if this is where you saw the reference to the Joint Command, you'll see that that's the heading of this document. That's how it starts. It's very prominent. Are you suggesting to us that in spite of receiving a document like that where that name was so prominently displayed, you had no interest in what this body might be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we understood this to be a document from the army or a result of some form of cooperation between the army and the police but I think we got it from the army. Military representatives at our meetings often shared information that was based on documents like these. Believe me, we believed this to be some form of organisation applied to their command posts. What we talked about, I couldn't be certain. I remember, or rather, when the document was shown to me, this jogged my memory. I saw the title, but believe me, members of the Working Group or me never looked into this. This was the sort of information that we received and it was useful, it was helpful. But this particular document was never closely inspected at any of our meetings with the army or the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about close inspection. I'm asking you about a clear, distinct, title of the body sending you the report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we didn't look into that. Our understanding was this was a document from the army or from the cooperation with the police because security information is being provided here. Believe me, we didn't investigate that. We thought this was how they organised their work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just to be absolutely clear, when you said "we," you are referring to Mr. Matkovic and Mr. Andjelkovic. They also --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: They also --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: We had these joint meetings with the army and the police, and I believe I've said this before, haven't I.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was going to ask about the meeting. You were just talking about this document and documents like this. Mr. Andjelkovic, Mr. Matkovic, and Mr. Sainovic also received these documents or you showed these documents to them when you got them?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: I think we received two or three copies perhaps. That's as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when you say "we received," who? We -- by "we," you mean Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Matkovic, Mr. Andjelkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: The three of us as the Working Group. I believe we received a copy or two possibly, and then Mr. Sainovic, to the extent that I remember, also received that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at 1197.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And because there are time constraints I will tell you that 1197 is a document similar to the last one, except that it is for the 20th of November, 1998, a different date and a report on different activities. But it is also a Joint Command operations report which is said to be strictly confidential, that includes reports on the intelligence situation in Kosovo. And I'd just like you to have a look on the first page of that document again, that's the first page in B/C/S -- sorry, and that's e-court page 1. See the cover of that document, what is written on that document?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Yes: "To Milomir Minic, personally."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm about to go back to this same topic. I have some questions about this last document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Minic, at your meetings was this document ever discussed before it was put together? Were you involved in the drafting of this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: This document was never discussed at any of our meetings with the army or the police. No information was ever provided and we were in no way ever involved in its drafting.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You saw the envelope which reads: "To Milomir Minic"?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And that's where the record was found. What does that tell you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: This tells me that someone was passing information along.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Does that mean that at those meetings that you attended - but we see that you didn't receive this because you weren't at the actual meeting - when you were at this meeting and received these what about this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is going to be leading based on -- or may I request through the Court that the questions be phrased not in a leading manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It sounded like it was going to be a leading question, Mr. Fila, so could you start again with that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The minutes are marked November and the envelope says: "To Milomir Minic, personally." Did you receive that document or not; if not, why not, explain why not?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: I never received this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's asked and answered. He said that he saw them, that he got them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that's surely not the end of the matter --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Because that answer came in the course of your cross-examination. Please proceed. Please answer that question, Mr. Minic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for these two documents that have been shown here, I never received them. A meeting took place with Slobodan Milosevic on the 29th of October, and there was our Working Group comprising Zoran Andjelkovic, Dusko Matkovic, and myself, and this was the end of it. Our work stopped there. I can state here under oath that after that meeting we never met again with anyone from the army or the police. Nikola Sainovic was appointed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Minic, the question was whether you received the document, and you've already told us you did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what did you mean when --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, my apologies. My apologies. I thought I was being very clear. If I may, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- When I was in Kosovo and Metohija in August, possibly September, sometimes we received these documents and I received a copy or two myself, as far as I can remember, and Nikola Sainovic received a separate copy. These documents that the Prosecutor showed me are not documents that I received. I only said that it does, indeed, read to Minic personally, but I didn't go to Kosovo and Metohija and I'm repeating this because I think it's important for the Chamber. The work of our group stopped on the 29th of August [as interpreted]. Nikola Sainovic was appointed to head the Commission for Cooperation with the OSCE, Zoran Andjelkovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but what you're saying is while you were working there you received documents like this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did they record meetings that you had attended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for this document, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you about the ones that you say you did receive, did they refer to meetings that you attended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, no, no. I apologise. We received this as information. It is obvious that we were receiving information from the other side. Had we been some sort of a Joint Command, we would not have been informing ourselves.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreters didn't hear the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you give us the end of your answer again, please: "It's obvious we were receiving information from the other side ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not review this information. We didn't adopt this information and we were not involved in the drafting of this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You said something, though, about a Joint Command at the end of the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This document was entitled "Joint Command" and I saw it, as I said, at the outset at the beginning of my testimony, I saw this reference before I'd ever heard of the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Excuse me, before my friend proceeds, just a matter of the transcript from those last questions. utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When did your work in Kosovo stop, Mr. Minic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 29th of October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I was very clear our work in Kosovo and Metohija stopped after the meeting with Slobodan Milosevic where the report of the implementation of the plan was reviewed, and this was on the 29th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After that we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We understand. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the interpretation service later please listen to the witness's answer on page 74, lines 1 through 6, and this is the answer that you're after. And I would like to press on with my questions, if I may, since we have an answer there that is incomplete.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Minic, I believe we've clarified this now. You never received the two documents that we showed because you weren't there in November. Now, the President is asking you about the documents that you did receive. Can you please explain this now. Could we please have this brought up again, a document that you did not receive, P1198.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: I have 826.

utterances.text: What are the first four words of that document? It says Joint Command KiM. What if it said to the Joint Command of KiM, would there be a difference?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: I believe that I've answered that question. Had we been a Joint Command, we would not have been sending reports to ourselves, would we?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. You didn't receive this document. What about the two that you did receive, how did you receive them? Please listen closely because we are getting to the core of the matter. This document was drafted in two ways: Someone brought it to you or you actually put it together. Which was it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: Someone delivered these documents. We didn't produce these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the person who delivered the documents, where did he come from, which area or which sector? What could he possibly have been professionally speaking?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: I think it was someone from the army, from the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In response to a question by the Prosecutor showing you what they believe are the minutes, this is P1468, would those -- well, yeah, bring the document up. We need page 1 of that document, P1468.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't think I showed him 1468. I can't see how that arises.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Oh well, my apologies then. I'll ask him without the document. No problem at all. I thought this was easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I showed you -- you told me several times that you saw those minutes, and the Prosecutor asked you about that. Is there a single reference in those minutes, whoever it was that produced them, that put them together, is there a single reference to you producing a document that looks like what the Prosecutor showed you, any reference to that at all?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR MINIC
utterances.text: No, not even the document that I did receive. There is not a single reference, not a single word about this document being produced or, indeed, that at any of our meetings with the army and the police where we exchanged information about current affairs and the situation, a document like this or its production was ever discussed, never, not once.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Minic, that completes your evidence; thank you for coming to give it. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is with great pleasure, Your Honours, that I announce that I have no further witnesses; and please believe me, I feel a whole lot better now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you now close your case subject to resolving the issues over written material and the expert evidence that will be led letter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If we could just use five minutes just now on one matter. Mr. Ackerman, I noticed that now for the fifth day in succession Mr. Pavkovic has not been here. Can you indicate to us when that situation is likely to change?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think he will be here at our next session, I guess on Tuesday. I don't know if Your Honour saw the medical report that was distributed yesterday, but he suffers from a back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- Injury. And sitting for long hours in this court is very difficult for him, and we had those very long sittings at the beginning of this session for two weeks in a row and I think it just got him down. I think he's been recovering. I haven't spoken to him. I've only, through other persons, I've suggested that up until now it really wasn't absolutely necessary for him to be here and I would appreciate him waving. But now that we are starting the Ojdanic case I think it is necessary for him to be here because we get into the military aspects of the case. I would hope we don't start anything beyond the opening statement today in the Ojdanic case just for that reason because I would like him to be here for the testimony, even though he has, I think, waived again for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will indeed hear some evidence today and we'll need to find a way of making sure that he has a transcript as well as a recording of the testimony he's not seeing. I think that's done in any event for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There's no transcript, Your Honour, that's -- that would have to be specially done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN

It's his presence of advising me, occasionally, about something that might have come out of the witness that we need to deal with that's important and we can't do that after he listens to a recording days down the road. That's just not going to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It won't be days down the road, Mr. Ackerman, it will be immediately after today's hearing it will be before the next hearing and I have no idea how long the next witness is going to last.

But there does remain the possibility of some longer sitting next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think if there was like one day of an extended sitting he can probably deal with that, it's just that many, many in a row that seem to get him down. As I told you, I have not discussed this fully with him at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY

utterances.text: So I'm giving you off the top of my head what I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
