utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President, and members of the Trial Chamber, and welcome to the continuation of the Defence case for General Ojdanic. I say "continuation" because much of the evidence that shows General Ojdanic to be innocent of the charges brought against him has already been presented in the Prosecution case through the testimony of witnesses such as General Aleksandar Vasiljevic, General Dusan Loncar, and exhibits such as the collegiums of the General Staff. We welcome this opportunity to take our turn and to present a comprehensive picture to the Trial Chamber of who General Dragoljub Ojdanic is, what he did before and during the war, and why he should be found not guilty of all the charges against him. It was 51 years ago in 1956 when, as a 15-year-old boy, Dragoljub Ojdanic joined the Yugoslav Army. He excelled at his studies at the military academy, attaining degrees all the up to master's level. He also excelled in the field and was the only soldier ever to serve at every level of the army, from cadet all the way up to the Chief of the General Staff. When he joined the army, General Ojdanic took an oath to defend his country, even at the cost of his own life, and he spent his entire life standing by that pledge serving his country selflessly at all times. After 41 years of service he found himself plunged into a war that he did not want and that he could not win. During the Defence case we're going to take you through the inner workings of the Yugoslav Army. Our witnesses include leaders from all the branches of the army, the land forces, the army, and the navy. Many of the witnesses who will testify in the Defence case knew General Ojdanic very well and for many years. They will described him as an honest, straightforward, decent man with a high disagree of professionalism and devoted to the institution and integrity of the Yugoslav Army. With General Ojdanic what you see is what you get, and what you will get during the Defence case is evidence that General Ojdanic never had knowledge of or participated in any general -- any joint criminal enterprise to depart -- to deport Albanians from Kosovo. While portrayed by the Prosecution as a person chosen by President Slobodan Milosevic to lead the army into war and into war crimes, the evidence will show something completely different. A review of the General Staff collegiums going back to 1997 and 1998 while he was still deputy Chief of the General Staff show that General Ojdanic expressed views that were more cautious than those of the man he succeeded, General Perisic. For example, on the 12th of December, 1997, he told General Perisic, General, I think that we must answer two questions. First, a response or proposal or our thoughts on how to address the Kosovo problem and for everybody to reach an agreement through dialogue. Therefore, no dreams of military operations or tackling the issue of Kosovo with military force. Three days later at another collegium on the 15th of December, 1997, he was even clearer when he said, When I was in Kosovo recently I met a large number of Serbs in whose heads only the war option was present all the time and fools like these can lead us into war, but I will not stand behind them. For example, General Ojdanic consistently opposed the use of the army in Kosovo, recommending that the fight against the KLA be maintained by the Ministry of the Interior. On the 4th of May, 1998, he said at a senior staff meeting that the shortest and fastest way to lose Kosovo was through war. On the 29th of June, 1998, he stated the following: I personally see diplomacy and politics as the only way out of this situation, and as a soldier I believe in this strongly. When General Ojdanic became the Chief of Staff of the General Staff at the end of November 1998, he spent his first day in office addressing the conference on the international law of war, which he had organised as deputy Chief of Staff. On that occasion he said the following: Obeying the rules of war alleviates the cruelties of war and facilitates the establishment of peace. And furthermore, it is in the best traditions of the Yugoslav Army to respect these rules that accord with a feeling of humanity when it comes to the treatment of the victims of war. On his third day in office in his post, General Ojdanic received General Drewienkiewicz and other representatives of the OSCE and pledged to cooperate with them. General Ojdanic's words and deeds in the days and months that followed showed that he truly meant what he said. In his comments at the collegium on the 17th of December, 1998, General Ojdanic stated that the members of the verification mission all have diplomatic status, and that is how they should be treated. They must not be treated roughly or disrespect fully. Their presence is the least-painless form of intrusion and we should not give them any reason to withdraw. General Ojdanic consistently upgraded the army's support for the Kosovo Verification Mission and constantly advocated full cooperation with it, even when others accused him of being anti-Serb and biased in favour of the KLA -- accused them of being anti-Serb. He saw this as a necessary measure to avoid war and regularly advocated cooperation with the international community as the only solution to the crisis in Kosovo. At one collegium meeting, General Ojdanic warned that adventurism or false patriotism, which results in wilful behaviour which goes against the resolutions or agreements must be severely penalised because such conduct could have fatal consequences, both for this country and for its people. You will also hear from many members of the General Staff, who will tell you that when he succeed -- General Ojdanic succeeded General Perisic he pursued his policies and kept on the personnel and generally continued to administer the army as the independent professional organisation it had become over the years. Since our defence case focuses on General Ojdanic as an individual you will be hearing from those who worked with him directly at the General Staff. In order to understand who those witnesses are and what their relationship to General Ojdanic was during 1998 and 1999, it is necessary to have a better understanding of the organisation of the General Staff itself. We will have General Branko Krga, chief of the intelligence deputy; his deputy, General Jovan Milanovic. From the security department you will hear testimony from General Geza Farkas, the chief; and his assistant, General Branko Gajic. General Milorad Obradovic during the war performed the functions of the commander of the 2nd Army and previously the chief of the operative staff sector and also assistant to the General Staff. General Vidoje Pantelic, assistant of the chief of the general staff for the rear, for logistics. General Spasoje Smiljanic, commander of the RVN PVO and previously chief of the operative staff. General Miodrag Simic, head of the land forces department. General Vlade Nonkovic, assistant chief for the navy. General Djordje Curcin, head of the first administration and with him four other individuals from the first administration. Spasoje Mucibabic, Dragan Paskas, and Stanisa Ivkovic. We will also hear testimony from General Ljubomir Andjelkovic, head of the department of reconnaissance and anti-aircraft activity. General Gojovic and Svetislav Ristic, both heads of the legal department in the period when General Perisic and General Ojdanic were the Chiefs of the General Staff. General Zlatoje Terzic, chief of the fourth administration for education. General Slobodan Kosovac, chief of the department for mobilisation. General Slobodan Petkovic, chief of the department for atomic and biological protection. Milivoje Novakovic and Nedjo Danilovic, both of them from the department for information and moral administration. Colonel Rade Cucak, our first witness, the head of the administration for the border. Colonel Nejovan Jovanovic, head of the department for cooperation with foreign military representatives. Two colonels from the cabinet of the Chief of General Staff, they are Milovan Vlajkovic and Milan Radoicic. General Branko Fezer, who is in charge of personnel, and General Uzelac, chief of the traffic department. These witnesses will tell you that this is a man who, to the best of their knowledge, never had any plan to expel the Albanians from Kosovo and that General Ojdanic never advocated or gave any indication of having any knowledge of or participation in any such plan. Indeed, there is much evidence to show that the General Staff believed that it was NATO and the KLA what wanted the Albanians to leave Kosovo, while it was in the interests of the army that they remain there. On the 3rd of April, 1999, General Branko Krga who will testify here sent General Ojdanic an intelligence report, stating that NATO would prefer it if the civilian population were to leave Kosovo in order to make its bombings more effective and facilitate the deployment of ground forces in Kosovo should the need arise. On the 7th of April, 1999, in a special public statement to the Albanians of Kosovo, General Ojdanic said: "Albanians, it is only a life together in commonality without hatred and contempt which can lead to a happier future, a care-free childhood for your children regardless of religion or ethnic affiliation. Let us all work together to restore peace to this land of ours." And then he said: "Go back to your homes and return to your everyday work. Do this today." These are the words of the man who the Prosecutor claims was part of a joint criminal enterprise to expel Albanians. At the collegium of the 9th of April, 1999, the General Staff agreed that the KLA was forcing the Albanian civilian population to move out of Kosovo in order to create a humanitarian crisis and thereby to accuse the Serbs of ethnic cleansing. They also expressed concern that the flow of refugees out of Kosovo would enable the infiltration of KLA fighters from Albania mixed up among the returning refugees. They decided to publicly encourage refugees to return to their homes. That same day General Ojdanic issued a directive stipulating that reception of refugees at the state border should be conducted in an organised fashion, that the army should assist other government organs with respect to the further care of the refugees, and that KLA infiltration among the returning refugees should be prevented and that international humanitarian law should be respected. Therefore, the evidence elicited from our witnesses and Yugoslav Army documents will show that General Ojdanic and the General Staff never favoured the expulsion of Albanians from Kosovo and that they saw it as something completely counter-productive to the national interest. In addition to proving that General Ojdanic never participated in or had knowledge of any plan to expel the Albanians from Kosovo we will demonstrate through witnesses and documents, showing that his actions during the war were in keeping with the highest traditions, not only of the Yugoslav Army but of international humanitarian law as well. It is important, however, for the Trial Chamber to gain an understanding of the times and conditions under which General Ojdanic performed his duties and worked and these are the sites and sounds from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia during the war. While we dissect General Ojdanic's words and deeds from the 24th of March until the end of the war in June 1999 in this courtroom, which is clean and well-lit, eight years after the fact, insulated and isolated from everything and everybody, we must always bear in mind that General Ojdanic was acting at a time of intensive bombing living in an underground command post from which he never emerged until the end of the war and he took positions to defend the people and property in his country. When viewed in that context what General Ojdanic did was nothing short of remarkable. While organising and commanding troops at levels never seen before, General Ojdanic issued order after order to ensure that people going to Kosovo were screened both physically and psychologically and that they had a working knowledge of humanitarian law and that paramilitary formations be forbidden. General Ojdanic also made sure that military court organs be mobilised at the beginning of the war, that reports of war crimes be compiled and followed up and addressed by the military justice system. As the war continued, he insisted that the military justice system upgrade its work and be accountable through upgraded reporting requirements. During the Defence case you will hear from the chief of the legal department, General Gojovic, and other witnesses who will testify to the orders issued by General Ojdanic and the efforts made by the military justice system under difficult circumstances to implement them. You will also hear evidence of how reports were sent up the chain of command and orders were sent down the chain of command. The Yugoslav Army had a bottom-to-top reporting system from the level of a company all the way up to the level of the General Staff. On the table that you have before you, you can see the way that information moved from the events on the ground up to the top-most level. The General Staff received combat reports from the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps on a daily basis during the war. Evidence has shown and will show that none of the specific crimes alleged in the indictment were ever brought to the attention of the General Staff. General Ojdanic had no knowledge of these specific crimes. When he did become aware in general of crimes being committed in Kosovo, General Ojdanic sprang into action. He called President Milosevic up on the same day he learnt that such crimes were widespread. Then he called General Pavkovic that same day and organised a meeting at the highest level to look into these crimes. General Ojdanic sent senior members of the General Staff, such as General Geza Farkas, General Vasiljevic, and General Gajic to Kosovo to find out what was going on there and to recommend ways of remedying the situation. He also issued order after order designed to promote the prevention and punishment of war crimes at a high level, and the orders were transmitted down the chain of command to the lowest levels. General Ojdanic matched words with action. He took action, and his actions were implemented in a consistent and persevering manner and this shows that General Ojdanic never participated in any joint criminal enterprise that he never condoned any crimes against civilians but quite the contrary that he took more than reasonable steps to prevent and punish war crimes in Kosovo. The evidence that you will hear over the next few weeks will demonstrate that General Ojdanic is not guilty of the crimes with which he is charged. We hope that you will get to know General Ojdanic during this part of the trial from documentary evidence, from the descriptions of the events by those who lived through them with General Ojdanic, as well as through expert testimony, and finally at the end of the Defence case through the testimony of General Ojdanic himself. Although he is retired now and the only post he holds is that of husband, father, and grandfather, he is the same man, guileless, straight-talking. The same man that he was during the war. He will tell you what he did and why he did it. Our entire Defence team is proud to represent General Ojdanic in this trial. May we call our first witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Your first witness is?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our first witness is Colonel Rade Cucak, chief of intelligence administration -- no, I apologise, chief of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear Mr. Visnjic because he's far away from the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I need to ask the Trial Chamber to allow us two things. One is to shorten the time allotted for this witness from three hours to two hours, even though in our initial 65 ter motion we asked for three hours for examination-in-chief. And our other request is to introduce Exhibit 3D991 through this witness. We sent notice quite late, that is to say yesterday, concerning this exhibit; however, it was impossible for us to plan everything because the timetable in this case is as subject to change as the weather in the Netherlands and I apologise for this. It was only yesterday that we had occasion to have a meaningful conversation with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it not inevitable that all your 65 ter times will be altered in view of the limitation there is on the time available for the presentation of the Defence case? I mean, that must follow, and I doubt if you expect us to refuse the first part of your motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, but perhaps we will have some motions of the opposite nature. So I was just counting on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but it might be an idea I think if counsel yet to present their cases were to adjust the estimate so that we don't run into the situation that we had with the last two or three witnesses, where the Prosecution were claiming that they were misled by an indication that a witness would give evidence for much longer than he actually did. So if better indications can be given in light of what we now expect to be a period occupied by the trial, and you alone will know you have arranged the time available, then that would be helpful to the Prosecution I'm quite sure. As far as the other matter is concerned, Mr. Stamp, do you have any comment about the introduction of 3D991?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, I have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that will be allowed. So can we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, I have another motion, and that is -- I think that the witness may come in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, he can stay where he is at the moment. He doesn't need to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So have this witness testify partly viva voce and partly pursuant to 92 ter statement which was disclosed to the Prosecution and does not deviate substantially from what they were put on notice in 65 ter. This is our manner of speeding up proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've no reason to think that we will not admit a 92 ter statement unless some point is taken against you. So you can take that as read unless for some reason that there is opposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that -- is that everything?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Cucak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of General Ojdanic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Would you please introduce yourself for the record.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: My name is Rade Cucak. I'm a retired colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Before you proceed with your testimony, I wish to ask you whether it's true that on the 17th of August, 2007, you gave a statement to the Ojdanic Defence team, which you also signed?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, I also signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that while preparing for this testimony --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear Mr. Visnjic's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that everything you stated in that statement is correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think that there is some problem in transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you ask the question again then, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is it true that while preparing for this testimony you reviewed and you read that statement?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm to me that everything stated in that statement is accurate, and if you were to testify here in this courtroom you would repeat everything stated in that statement?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes, I confirmed that. I would state the same were I to testify here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is Exhibit 3D1083, the statement of the witness that we wish to tender under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, would you please tell us what was the last post you held before retirement?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Immediately before retiring I was chief of service for the state border within the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And what was your post during 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: During that time I was chief of service for the state border, or rather, department for border affairs within the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, and this department was located within the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the end of the sentence. Could the witness please come closer to the microphone, and the same applies to Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You told us where your department was located. Could you repeat what you said about where the department was located.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last post I held, or rather, the one before the last was my post as chief of the department for border affairs within the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And the department for border -- I apologise. The department for border service was within which administration within the General Staff of the army Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: That department was within the first administration or operations administration, as it is also known, of the sector for operational and staff affairs of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement you described in detail your career, however, during one collegiums General Marjanovic announced you as the man who slept at least three times in each border post. Please tell me, how much time did you spend at the border dealing with border affairs?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: When I started working back in 1987 in the department for border affairs, I was an officer for border affairs from then on until 2000. I served in the General Staff holding all posts, including the highest one which is the chief of border service. Throughout that time I dealt with organisational and technical matters as well as inspecting the border regime; that is to say that I spent quite a lot of time at various borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In your statement you described quite in detail the terms and the regime of securing the state border. Could you please confirm what was said in paragraph 8 of your statement and to give us some features of the border between the Republic of Albania and Republic of Macedonia with FRY that have to do directly with the system of securing the state border.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: I gave some basic features of the state border with Albania and Macedonia; however, the state border with Albania and Macedonia, the borderline runs along high mountain range, high above the sea level, and the range splits it into two. The border is basically inaccessible, although there are some routes that one can take in order to cross on foot and unlike the border with Macedonia -- unlike the border with Albania, the border with Macedonia is a bit more accessible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You wanted to add something else.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: The border as it was needed sufficient troops to secure it, especially during the time when it was quite difficult, in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Were there any parts of the border that had not been regulated by state treaties?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes. The border with the newly established states in the territory of the former Yugoslavia was not regulated by any state treaties so that the border between Kosovo and Macedonia, or rather, the entire border with Macedonia was not regulated by an international treaty, but the delineation process began.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I think that you were appointed chief in 1995, am I right?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What did you encounter, what was the situation like when you came --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before we go into that, Mr. Visnjic, looking at paragraph 8 - and I'd like you just to help me with this rather than ask the witness if you can - you refer -- the statement refers to three passes through the mountain between Albania and the FRY. And then the next paragraph mentions routes running across the border. Now, do these go through the passes that are mentioned in the previous paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it would be best if the witness answers that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean you're unable to answer? I mean, I can understand that but you'll appreciate it if --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you don't know the answer to that, you're going to understand that we're going to be even more in the dark unless it's clarified, and it may be of some importance because of the evidence that we've heard about the routes that refugees claim to have taken. So please ask the witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for not answering immediately. I'm just waiting for interpretation to conclude; that's why I'm not reacting immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, please tell the Court in relation to the border between Kosovo and the Republic of Albania, first of all, what are the official roads? Please look at your statement, paragraph 8. We're now speaking of the roads between the Republic of Albania and Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: The border passes Cafa Prusit, Cafa Dobrunes, and Morina are the passes along which the roads run, across which the roads run.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Which ones are related to the state border -- just a minute, Colonel. Which road runs along which pass because sometimes there's several settlements with the same name. So could you tell the Court which road runs along which pass?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Cafa Prusit is Cafa Prusit, that road and that pass. Vrbica going along Zijaz, this is not up in the mountains. This is a road leading from the Federal Republic into Albania and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Connecting which two major towns?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Well, you have it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If you could just tell us, please. Colonel, take it easy, please, explain to the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think if I could just stop you there. I think -- and please listen to I'm going to say and if I've got the picture clearly. You were referring first of all to three mountain passes. You then followed that by reference to three roads which are not through the mountain passes and one railway. And then you then followed that by the names of the three crossings for the specific roads and the railway. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's correct that there are three border crossings to Albania; these are mentioned in my statement. Vrbica, Cafa Prusit, and Bozaj. And there's another railway crossing. These -- this is Tuzi, too, from Kosovo and Metohija Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, from Kosovo and Metohija -- and one from Montenegro to Albania, the road, and the railway from Tuzi to Albania.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Just continue, please, Mr. Visnjic. I'll have a look at the map later.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Could you please describe the border. You started by saying that the border crosses a mountain range. Could you please wait until I finish my question. You started by saying that the border crosses a number of mountain ranges. Please, if you have anything to add, feel free to do so.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: The border, the Albanian border, crosses some mountain ranges, the Junik Mountain, Pastrik, and Gora and then on to Macedonia and across to Mount Sara. This border is a difficult one to cross although there are many footpaths there, according to our estimate over 200 of those and it's possible to move along those and four people to walk across the state border using those footpaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Throughout 1998 -- actually I'm talking about the first half of 1998, what was the security system along the state border on the Kosovo side facing Albania and Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: The security regime along the state border was stepped-up back in 1995, and this applied throughout until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "stepped-up" in relation to the security regime along the state border?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Stepped-up security regime means that people worked 12-hour shifts and more, up to 16-hour shifts in certain areas. A minor part work eight-hour shifts and then they take a rest. This required a lot of men in order to get the state border secured, those who were fit to do so, of course, and were trained to perform that sort of task.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have Exhibit 3D182.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you've heard of the so-called White Book of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, have you not? This is about incidents that occurred along the border throughout the period that we are referring to in 1995, 1996, 1997, 1998, 1999. I believe we actually looked at the book as you were being prepped for your testimony, right?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You went through the incidents enumerated in that book, right?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, who was the source of information for what is presented in the book?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: As for border incidents, the source was the General Staff of the VJ. The General Staff obtained its information from the Pristina Corps, the command of the 3rd Army, in the form of daily operative reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have page 85 brought up on our monitors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the same exhibit, 3D182.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, we see an example here, several of those incidents. This refers to May 1998. What I wanted to ask you is this: In addition to this material that was probably provided at a later stage to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, did the VJ also prepare a file in which it tried to list all the incidents along the state border, especially the border to Albania? Are you familiar with that, that is, between January and June 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with that. The Army of Yugoslavia periodically reported to the relevant state bodies on the situation along the state border. In this period, too, they drew up a report for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs so that they might then inform the domestic and international public about what was going on along the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 3D991.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, a document is about to appear in front of you from the Pristina Corps command dated the 17th of April, 1998. Could you please have a look and then comment on it if you can. It's not necessarily for you to repeat what the document actually says. Just comment, please, comment on the substance of this document. You will soon see page 1. While you're looking at it, let me ask you one question: Are you familiar with this particular incident?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this incident that occurred on the 17th of April, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you comment on the development described in this document?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: It was sometime past midnight on the 16th of April or perhaps the early morning hours. It was 1.45 a.m. A group of between 50 and 60 people carried out an attack from the territory of the Republic of Albania. They organised an ambush and attack from the territory of the Republic of Albania, a terrorist group --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But don't read the document. Comment, please.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: They opened fire from the territory of the Republic of Albania and they fired at official state border bodies of Yugoslavia who were securing the border. An attempt was made to force their way into the Yugoslav territory and to create conditions for bringing in weapons and military equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: There are preferences in this document to -- there is a reference to a code LMK. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: The code LMK is an abbreviation which means local mixed commission. It's a joint local mixed commission of Yugoslavia and Albania. That's what it means. It comprises a Yugoslav part and an Albanian part.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the commission go to the scene of the incident?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes. Joint on-site inspection was carried out and they found some weapons and military equipment in that area. However, the Albanian side started to react by saying that those incidents had occurred from Albanian territory. So when the Yugoslav state patrols said that they would fire at the area from which the action had arrived, the Albanian part of the joint commission requested or demanded that this not be done, which only proves that they knew about the incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that an accurate translation that the Albanian side started to react by saying that those incidents had occurred from Albanian territory?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the document or what the witness just said, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's what the witness said. He said at line 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was action from Albanian territory because the group virtually had entered territory, but they had received support from Albanian territory, the territory of the state of Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let me phrase it this way. What did the Albanian side acknowledge or accept, if you like?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: They did not deny when they saw the amount of weapons and military equipment; however, they said that the Albanian side was not responsible for this. They also denied that the perpetrators were from Albanian territory. That is the essence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How did you conclude that they were supporting these persons who committed the incident? How did you conclude that the Albanian side were supporting these people who were purportedly operating from Albania?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Because the border bodies, our president [as interpreted] of the joint local commission -- for many reasons, actually. The people who experienced this were the organs who involved in this event and they told everybody about it. Secondly, at an LMK meeting a member of our joint commission, our representative of the local mixed commission announced that fire would be opened at the facility and at the territory that had been used to attack Serbia, or rather, Yugoslavia. And then the Albanian representative in the local commission reacted vehemently and ask that this not be done, which was proof, although the firing was not accidental, that they knew who was in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's something peculiar about line 5 on that page. It may have been something like representative of the joint local commission but it certainly our president; however, it will no doubt be corrected in the review. Please continue, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can we please now move on to 3D738.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you testified that the army was reporting to state bodies about these incidents. Can you please look at this document, sir, and tell us briefly whether you're familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this document. This is a report, information, that was sent to the minister of foreign affairs because of everything that was going on along the state border between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be enlarged for the witness. Can we please zoom-in on the last three paragraphs, the last three passages in paragraph 1, the last three lines, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This statement or proposal that the Republic of Albania be indicted in front of the relevant national institutions for their support to Siptar separatists and terrorists and for an open act of aggression against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, I would say this is a very serious charge.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes. This is, indeed, a very serious charge, but it is true, the reason being, although serious border incidents were committed from Albania territory sabotage and terrorist groups were crossing from Albania's territory they enjoyed their tacit support and the Albanian side did absolutely nothing in order to suppress these incidents and in order to keep the Yugoslav state border from being threatened which would have been in keeping with the agreement. Another thing that is important is that the Yugoslav side at the time many times spoke to the Albanian side in order to set up a joint local commission for these violations of the state border. The commission was not set up at the time and never has been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the date of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 16th of July, 1998. May we now have page 2 of the document shown to the witness, paragraphs 2, 3, and 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: May we have your comments on those three paragraphs. The one beginning: "Albania fully placed its territory ..." Et cetera and the following two paragraphs, so paragraph 1, 2, and 3.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: In the piece of information something that was quite obvious was stressed. It was impossible that on a daily basis masses of armed persons wearing different uniforms and civilians, too, be moving in all directions without anybody from the official Albanian organs reacting. So it was tacit support to the terrorist forces on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In addition to this covert support, other forms of support were also mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes. The authorities determined this by monitoring the situation. They determined that cadres were being trained in Albania and that they were being armed, and that a lot of the weapons that these people carried were the same as the weapons that the Albanian army had. So how could they have reached the hands of Albanian terrorists unless they were being supplied. And we know that all the barracks in 1997 were pilfered on the territory of Albania and all the outposts, too, and there was no security system for the borders. And somehow these weapons found their way into the hands of the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, everybody is tired, so please slow down. I'm sure you'll understand, we're all tired and so are the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This piece of information was signed by the Chief of the General Staff, who was General Perisic at the time, of the JNA. Do you know what prompted him to give out this piece of information and is it linked to any other activities that the Yugoslav Army performed at that time and linked to the situation and regime or system along the state border?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: This was signed by the Chief of the General Staff. He had to sign it in order to let the international community know what was going on and not to blame a country that was defending itself from terrorist forces in the area being blamed and that measures be taken, adequate measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is that the slowest you can go?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Well, I'll do my best to speak slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit 3D740 next, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: While we're awaiting that if we can go back one Exhibit, Mr. Visnjic, 3D991, is there no English version of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There was. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 9 of the summary you speak about the extension of the border belt and I'll show you 3D740 next, that exhibit, it is the Official Gazette in which the decision was published to -- on the determination and establishment of the border areas. It is dated the 21st of July, 1998. Now, Colonel, when we compare this document and the document of the 16th of July, 1998, the letter to Zivadin Jovanovic, can you explain to the Court why such a decision was taken in the first place, who proposed it, and how was the decision put into practice on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: The Zivadin Jovanovic letter is a product of the situation on the ground. As I've already said, it was designed to inform the international community and also the local public, domestic public, about the situation. At the same time, the competent state authorities looked into measures that could be undertaken to ensure that the state border was secure and that was their role as state organs. And in order to achieve that, the operative department, after consulting the -- those who implemented the security system on the ground came to the conclusion that what was needed was to extend the border belt, to expand it towards Albania in order to create conditions for the security system to function properly, more easily, or rather, to apply tactics in the security system and to reduce the effects that the terrorist activities had on the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell us what this actually meant in practice. Give us an example.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Well, this is what it meant in practice. The border belt was a belt of 100 metres facing Albania, the border towards Albania. And from the territory of Albania on several occasions the person at the border providing security was targeted on a number of occasions. The security organs were not able to organise other forms of protection and security like reconnaissance posts, observation posts, or things like that, and so the border belt was expanded to allow the security forces to be able to control a broader area and move around a broader area, in conformity with the law of course, and to be able to provide proper security and protection for the border belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Shall we take a look at what this was like on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D739 is the next exhibit, it is a map which is on e-court, but we have brought a copy with us here into court and I hope that it will give you a better overview of the situation and area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, we have the legend. The yellow is the expansion of the border belt in July 1998, is it not. Now, can you explain the differences in width, or rather, depth on this border belt when we look at it on the map when we see the borders with Albania and Macedonia. But tell me, first of all, whether this expansion related to the entire border of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, all its borders.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: There was an expansion of the border belt before this, too, in certain sections of the border belt during the SFRY, some of these were retained. After that the border belt was expanded towards Albania, that's the first expansion, and this was in line with the assessments on a need-to-do basis and this is the area where there was -- where there were -- which was shot at. There was firing in all these areas as well as at Lake Skadar, which --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Which is the border with Montenegro, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: This is the border between Albania and Yugoslavia on the territory of Montenegro. So where the border was most endangered and where the border regime was violated on many occasions and where there was shooting, what we did was to expand the border belt in depth and that we looked at the roads, too. It was very difficult to cross certain mountains, so mountain passes and paths were -- the passage through these areas were facilitated. So the border was not 5 kilometres, it was 500 metres towards Bojana and 3 to 5 kilometres in this area, the higher mountains and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I clarify something. Mr. Visnjic said to you that the yellow part was the extension. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct. That is the extension of the border belt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is the red line the border?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The red line -- this line is the border. This is the border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does -- excuse -- excuse our ignorance, but we need to be clear about this. Does that mean that the border belt, as you have called it, does not normally go up to the border?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It does. The border belt does go up to the border, it's just an extended border belt. It's -- the border belt established by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was a belt of 100 metres and that came under the authority of the security organs, but the law also provided for the fact that -- or for the possibility of extending the border belt where necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, does that mean that you established the border on the territory of Albania? I know that sounds stupid, but I have to say I don't understand this. If the yellow part is the extension, it follows that the grey part is what was originally the border belt, and that doesn't appear to go to the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, might I be allowed to help out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The thin red line is the border between Albania and Yugoslavia. A thicker yellow line continues on from this line, which was the first extension of the border belt. The second extension of the border belt from March 1999 - and we'll come to that in due course during the examination of this witness - is the second red line, if I can call it that, but it's pink actually, which follows on from the yellow line, the thicker pink or red line or belt, whichever you like to call it, following on from the yellow one. So all the extensions go towards Yugoslav territory, whereas the thin red line is the beginning of the border and the actual border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That now clarifies it, but without being told what the border was and without being told what the pink area was, it was not easy to understand this. Now I do understand this, so please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: One more clarification. Did you also have a buffer zone within the belt or before the belt or the belt was the buffer zone itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The buffer belt did not exist. The borderline was the borderline, which was to be respected and abided by both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would like also to understand why it was necessary to extend an area that has a name "border belt." By doing that what was it you could do on that territory that you could not previously do on that territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First let me give you the basics. First of all, we prevented direct shooting at people from Albanian territory, because we had a number of direct attacks using fire-arms, shooting the security people moving along the border belt. Second, we created conditions to apply different tactics, security tactics by which the security organs can move around -- could move around undetected, and thereby to register a people violating the border regime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that you've said that already in your statement, but why could you not do these things anyway without declaring an extension to the border belt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say that people were killed in that border belt, I have to add that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but what was it that you were prevented from doing to deal with that without extending the border belt? What actions could you not take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were not able to have an aggression against Albania, clean-up all the area around the border was it was an area of aggression and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia did not want to have this kind of aggression. The terrorists had crossed the border --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can't have aggression on your own territory. But maybe you can help, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, tell me, please, what were the powers of the army in the border belt and what were the powers of the army outside the border belt?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: The army in the border belt had the following rights: To ask for ID of any people who violated the border regime and crossed over unlawfully, to arrest them, and to hand them over to the competent organs of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let's take this step by step. When an individual who violates the border regime exits this 100-metre border belt, what powers did the army have, if it had any? What could the army do about it?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: The army had the power, if they noticed somebody crossing unlawfully, to follow them until they arrest them and then hand them over to the competent authorities. That is by the book. However, on rare occasions the -- it was rare that organs entered the territory, but when there was shooting in the border belt if they were not able to pass by unnoticed they would go back to Albanian territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, the army outside the border belt, did it have the right to set up ambushes and other forms of border control?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: No. Only if the unit was in the border belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the basis then for saying that the army cannot do that without extending the border belt? Why can't the army just exercise reasonable force to prevent attacks on the territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The army, the border units, could not. They were not authorised to fire upon the territory of Albania. This 100-metre belt did not allow them to move around safely, to stay there safely. For that reason, the border belt was extended so that the border patrol could inspect the territory deeper in than just the border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My reason for being particularly concerned about this is in case it has some relevance for the issues over General Perisic's attitude to the powers of the army. Unless we understand this, then it is going to be difficult for us to deal with that issue. And at that moment, the only thing that the witness appears to have said - and I doubt if he really means it - is that if you extend the border belt you can start shooting at Albanians in Albania.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, absolutely that's not -- that wasn't stated. That's not the case. The witness said that the border belt is extended in order to create conditions for the border security to do their job in their own territory, for them to have legal powers and not to fire upon anybody else's territory or the state territory of Albania or the territory of any other state for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The one other possibility in what you've said is that if somebody manages to get over the border belt then you can't actually arrest them. But, you see, I suspect that's not right either. So I'm not understanding at all what it is you can do that you couldn't do before the border belt was extended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, I would also like to add something, maybe it clarifies. Was it an extended area where you had a sort of a curfew, where you checked people much beyond the border, and if anybody entered that curfew territory then he must have papers or -- was that the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I have to repeat yet again. The border belt is part of the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, where the state border organs have certain powers. They can ask for IDs, they can search, they can detain somebody and hand them over to competent state organs. That is to say, that applies to the belt. Why did we extend it? Well, we extended it because we could not deploy our people within that 100-metre belt and have them shot at from the Albanian territory and killed, because that's what was happening. In order for us to prevent fire being opened from the territory of Albania, we extended the border belt so that our people could be deeper inside our own territory and thus be safe from the fire opened from -- opened at them from the territory of Albania and so that they could patrol the area and prevent the people from entering the territory of Yugoslavia illegally and bringing in with them a large amount of illegally obtained weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean that you're saying the state border organs have no powers out with the border belt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely that. Their powers are linked to the border belt solely, unless they're chasing somebody. And they can chase somebody only until they hand them over to the MUP representatives. They can only chase somebody within their own territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown P1440, page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, please tell me, after the border belt was extended, did the situation improve at the border?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the situation did not improve significantly, except that the state, or rather, the security organs were given a broader territory where they could act and they uncovered or detected more violators than previously, violators who were bringing in from the territory of Albania various kinds of military equipment, arms, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, would you please look at the document before you. Are you familiar with this event?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you comment, please?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes. This involved a unit which came to secure the state border. Every unit entering the area of the border belt for official purposes has to first become familiar with the area where they're going to serve, where they're going to move, and they need to become familiar with the most frequent offences in that border belt and the reasons why the border belt is at risk. This unit came to the border belt and its commander wished to take them through the border belt, once, twice, if necessary, three times in order for them to become familiar with the terrain so that they could work independently in the border belt. Unfortunately, on that day an ambush was organised partially in the territory of Albania and partial in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And the border organs which were closer to the border were ambushed and then the document describes the consequences that ensued.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown 3D663, Exhibit 3D663. These are minutes from the collegium of the Chiefs of General Staff from the 3rd of November, 1998. Could the witness please be shown page 20 in B/C/S, paragraph 2; in English page 9, paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you were present at this meeting, you attended the collegium, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly, there was a discussion about the border. What was the importance of the border for Yugoslavia at that point in time; that is to say, to what extent the border problems represented a significant problem?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: The border between Kosovo and Metohija and the neighbouring states was burdened by terrorist activities and it was endangered significantly. That required significant amount of troops and resources, which needed to be sent to the area in order to prevent any losses on our side inflicted by the terrorist forces who were active. Unfortunately, in this period of time the terrorists became active internally as well in the settlements within the border area. They started attacking border organs and border units stationed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you say internally, what do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: From the territory of Serbia and Montenegro, from Kosovo. Those were the terrorist forces that were inside the country. I have to explain this so that it's clear. As soon as the border belt was extended, it became more difficult to bring in weapons and military equipment into the country. In order to distract the border organs, the terrorist forces active in Kosovo and Metohija occasionally would attack border organs from our own territory, from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, that is to say territory of Serbia and Yugoslavia. They would attack border organs in order to create a confusion and to enable them to bring in further quantities of military equipment and weapons. And that was one of the reasons that the meeting of the collegium was held, in order to draw attention to these problems and to see what steps needed to be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can stay on the same page, page 20, paragraph 7 in B/C/S, but in English it's page 10, paragraph 5. Colonel, General Perisic talks here about the need to secure the state border. What was his position at that point?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: General Perisic insisted on securing the border with existing forces and resources. He insisted on other units being deployed there, if necessary from the Pristina Corps and -- but not the, or rather, he -- I always insisted on specially trained personnel to be sent to the border belt because that is my position, that only people that are specially trained for that could serve in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If I understood you well, there was a proposal to deploy to the border belt special units, or rather, not special units, but rather, units trained for border inspection?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: At this meeting of the collegium, we wanted -- as I've told you earlier, we started having terrorist activity inside the country, in the border belt, and we wanted to create conditions for our units to act without hindrance in the border belt. We wanted to ensure that they were safe, that nobody would attack them from their backs. This is why we proposed that the border belt be additionally extended in order to create legally a situation where only people who were specially authorised could stay in that area or people who had their residence there and who were specially registered by the organs and who were then allowed to stay in the extended border area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And as far as I could gather- and you can see that here in paragraph -- in the last paragraph of page 10 of the English and page 11, paragraph 1 and 2 of B/C/S General Perisic proposed this and what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Well, this was on the 3rd of November. General Perisic rejected this proposal, but then only for the reasons known to him he went to Kosovo and Metohija on the second -- on the following day, on the 4th of November, and he came to the forward command post in Djakovica and there he met with the commander of the forward command post. He was briefed about the situation there and he could see himself the problems that existed concerning securing the state border. Then upon his return, he changed his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: He said that appropriate measures needed to be taken in order to build up the security system and in order to create conditions for people to be able to live and work there, for the services that were stationed there to be able to work there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if General Perisic issued any orders related to that?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes. Following that, he ordered that a special team be created to analyse the situation in detail, a team of experts, and then to propose appropriate solutions. This expert team, as far as I can remember, comprised Chief of Staff of the 3rd Army, General Simic; Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps, now - General Lazarevic, at the time he was a Colonel; and some other expert organs that dealt with the issues of securing the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know if this is a good time to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Cucak, we have to terminate our proceedings for the day at this stage; that means that you will have to come back here on Monday to continue your evidence. That will be at 9.00 on Monday morning --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it's on Tuesday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, yes, sorry, on Tuesday. I apologise. Tuesday morning at 9.00. Over the weekend and until you come back here to continue your evidence, you must have no discussion with anyone at all about the evidence in this case. You can meet with and talk with whoever you wish about other things, but not the evidence in the case. Now would you please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will now adjourn until 9.00 on Tuesday, but the final sitting arrangements for Tuesday and Thursday will be notified to you sometime in the course of Monday. The start time will not change, but it may be that the full sitting times will change. So 9.00 on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
